Abstract:
<jats:p>Melt-pool depth governs interlayer bonding and porosity in laser powder bed fusion and underpins part qualification, yet predicting it reliably remains difficult. Fast conduction models reach useful accuracy only after the absorptivity is fitted to the depths they are meant to predict, and inverse analyses have been used the same way, to recover a calibrated parameter rather than to test the model. Here, the absorptivity is fixed independently instead, a measured coupling for IN718 and, for IN625 and 316L, a published closed-form relation never fitted to the present depths. This converts a moving-source conduction model from an object of calibration into one of validation. The melt boundary is located by root-finding rather than on a grid, so no discretization error enters the diagnosis. Across 231 single tracks, the model reproduces conduction-regime depth and half-width to within a few percent and underpredicts increasingly once keyholing begins. Inverting each measured depth for the absorptivity conduction would require yielding a fitting-free diagnosis: no conduction-regime track demands a non-physical value, and the inferred value converges near 0.38 against inputs of 0.27 to 0.34, whereas every keyhole-classified track demands a value above unity. Because an inferred absorptivity also absorbs unmodeled transport, downward convection was emulated as an anisotropic effective diffusivity; at the enhancement reported for Marangoni flow, no keyhole track becomes explicable. A measured Ti-6Al-4V absorptivity rise of a factor 1.9 supports the mechanism. An enthalpy-indexed correction and data-driven baselines remain alloy-specific, whereas the physics-based model retains its advantage under cross-alloy extrapolation. All findings are for single tracks on bare plates.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Significant advances have been made in the field of Additive Manufacturing (AM) across various manufacturing processes. Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) is one of the most widely adopted metal AM processes in the industry, which employs energy sources such as lasers to melt powder materials. While the LPBF process offers numerous advantages, such as the ability to produce complex geometries and multiple parts simultaneously, it also presents challenges in the form of defects such as porosity, residual stresses, and cracks that need to be addressed. Conducting experiments to identify and eliminate these defects can be prohibitively expensive, motivating the development of alternative predictive approaches. Numerical modeling and simulation techniques provide a cost-effective alternative to experimental approaches, enabling analyses ranging from thermal histories and microstructural evolution to mechanical property prediction and defect identification in fabricated components. However, such simulations can also be computationally intensive. In recent years, Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) algorithms have emerged as viable alternative tools to accelerate process understanding, defect prediction, and parameter optimization. This review provides a comprehensive overview of ML-based approaches applied to LPBF, emphasizing the importance of understanding the underlying physical phenomena that significantly influence data collection, preprocessing, and feature engineering strategies essential for effective model training and validation. It offers a structured framework for researchers seeking to leverage ML methods to enhance predictive accuracy and computational efficiency, particularly through simulation-driven data generation for model development.</jats:p>

The excerpt describes complementary approaches for characterizing LPBF spatter and vapor-plume behavior in aluminum alloys. High-speed optical and Schlieren imaging have been used to observe spatter and the vapor plume above the powder surface, but these methods do not provide detailed information about changes in vapor-depression or keyhole morphology. High-speed synchrotron x-ray imaging addresses this limitation by capturing both melt-pool/keyhole dynamics and spatter, with temporal resolution reported as high as 1 MHz. The study quantifies spatter number, trajectory angle, velocity, and kinetic energy, and relates ejection angle to depression-zone/keyhole morphology. The abstract identifies distinct behavior associated with melting mode: conduction-mode vapor pressure produces backward spatter, while the keyhole rear wall redirects gas/vapor flow and produces more vertical ejection and rear-rim droplet spatter. The excerpt does not specify camera models, illumination systems, or conventional optical frame rates, nor does it provide a direct aluminum-versus-steel comparison. It does establish the quality relevance: oversized spatter can increase surface defects and roughness, become trapped in later layers and cause lack-of-fusion porosity, oxidize powder, inhibit fusion, and reduce part density. Small spatter can also induce powder denudation and surface cavities after laser-spatter interaction.

function.arguments: {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a comprehensive table summarizing the 9 measurement categories for LPBF Al and Cu alloy characterization. For each category, include: Measurement, Method(s)/Equipment, Key Standards, Sample Requirements, Key Equations/Criteria, Typical Uncertainties, and key Published Example DOIs. Categories: 1) Melt pool geometry, 2) Laser absorptivity, 3) Thermal history/cooling rate, 4) CET/grain structure, 5) Composition change, 6) Printability maps, 7) Residual stress, 8) Spatter/plume, 9) Powder properties."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| # | Measurement | Method(s) / typical equipment | Key standards | Sample requirements | Key equations / criteria | Typical uncertainty / limitation | Published examples |
|---:|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Melt-pool width, depth, length and melting mode | Optical/SEM top views; transverse and longitudinal metallographic sections; calibrated microscope and ImageJ/Fiji; optional coaxial or off-axis high-speed imaging. Mount, grind and polish; etch Al with Keller’s or Weck’s reagent and Cu alloys with FeCl₃–HCl, ammonium persulfate or Klemm-type reagent after alloy-specific trials. Measure at least 3 transverse sections per track—preferably 5–8—and one longitudinal section; omit acceleration/deceleration zones. | ASTM E3 and E407; ASTM E112 where grain size is also measured | Approximately 20–40 parameter combinations; 2 replicate tracks per condition; tracks ≥5–10 mm. Use a bare plate and a nominal powder layer where possible because coupling differs. | Aspect ratio: `AR = d/w`; conduction generally `d/w < 0.5`, transition near 0.5, keyhole generally `d/w > 0.5`. King criterion is equivalently `d/(w/2) > 1`; reported normalized-enthalpy transition `ΔH/h_s ≈ 30 ± 4`. LOF risk if `d < t`; overlap criterion `(h/w)² + (t/d)² ≤ 1`. Fit absorptivity and, only if independently uncertain, beam radius by minimizing weighted width/depth/length residuals; validate on held-out tracks. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000033) | Well-polished cross-sections commonly give ±2–5 µm edge-location error and 5–10% repeatability; along-track instability can dominate, especially in transition/keyhole mode. A single section is inadequate. | King et al., **10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2014.06.005**; Caprio et al., **10.3390/met12101762**; Tenbrock et al., **10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2019.116514**; Bergmueller et al., **10.1007/s00170-023-11377-2** |
| 2 | Effective laser absorptivity at approximately 1070 nm | **Calorimetry:** thermally isolated metal disk or coupon, embedded thermocouples, known heat capacity and laser trajectory; compare temperature rise with incident energy. **Integrating sphere:** gold-coated sphere, calibrated InGaAs detectors for sphere and back-reflected channels, reference diffuse-gold target; sub-microsecond acquisition is possible. Test polished bulk, as-received surface and controlled powder layers separately. | Detector calibration traceable to radiometric standards; no single LPBF-specific absorptivity standard | At least 3 repeats for each surface state and several power–speed conditions spanning no melt, conduction, transition and keyhole. Trapp used approximately 100 µm powder layers. | `A_eff = E_abs/E_L`; calorimetry: `E_abs = m∫C_p(T)dT`, `E_L = P L/v`; sphere: `A(t) = 1 − [P_sphere(t)+P_head(t)]/P_0(t)` when transmission is negligible. Clean bulk Cu is about 0.03–0.05 and loose Cu powder about 0.12–0.20 at low intensity; measured Cu powder rose toward approximately 0.53 near keyholing. Powder and keyhole values must not be replaced by room-temperature Fresnel data. (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010) | Calorimetry typically about ±5–10% relative after heat-loss correction; integrating-sphere radiometry can reach a few percent after port, filter and detector calibration. Calorimetry may underestimate coupling if vaporized/ejected mass carries unmeasured enthalpy. | Trapp et al., **10.1016/j.apmt.2017.08.006**; Simonds et al., **10.1103/PhysRevApplied.10.044061**; Gargalis et al., **10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2021.117130**; Ye et al., **10.1002/adem.201900185** |
| 3 | Thermal history, peak temperature, thermal gradient `G`, solidification rate `R` and cooling rate | Fine K- or N-type thermocouples embedded in substrate near tracks; two-colour pyrometer; calibrated MWIR/SWIR high-speed camera with spectral filters; post-mortem SEM measurement of cellular or dendrite-arm spacing; high-speed synchrotron radiography/diffraction for melt boundary, keyhole and solidification front. | ITS-90 traceability for temperature calibration; ASTM E230/E230M for thermocouples | ≥3 instrumented repeats per representative condition; use several known camera/pyrometer calibration temperatures. For spacing proxies, measure ≥100 intercepts or cells across pool boundary, centre and trailing region on ≥3 tracks. | `R = v cosθ`, where `θ` is between scan direction and local interface normal/growth direction; `Ṫ = G R`; spacing proxy `λ = A(Ṫ)^{-n}`. Determine `A,n` for the specific alloy/microstructural metric rather than importing a casting correlation. LPBF Al commonly lies around `10⁵–10⁷ K s⁻¹`. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020) | Embedded thermocouples are bandwidth- and distance-limited and may under-read melt temperature by hundreds of kelvin. Two-colour pyrometry commonly ±2–5% if grey-body assumptions hold; single-colour IR can be wrong by >10% without dynamic emissivity. Spacing-derived cooling rate is often uncertain by a factor of approximately 2–3. | Guo et al., **10.1016/j.addma.2019.04.021**; Huang et al., **10.1038/s41467-022-28694-x**; Soderlind et al., **10.3390/cryst12101437**; Rahman et al., **10.3390/machines13020160** |
| 4 | Columnar-to-equiaxed transition, grain size and crystallographic texture | EBSD on longitudinal build/scan sections and pad top surfaces; field-emission SEM with EBSD detector; optional EDS/TEM for Al₃(Sc,Zr). Final polish with colloidal silica or low-energy ion milling. Map entire melt pools at coarse step and boundary/centre regions at ≤0.05–0.2 µm for submicrometre Sc/Zr-refined grains. | ASTM E2627 for EBSD orientation analysis; ASTM E112 for conventional grain size | ≥3 melt pools or tracks per condition; ≥3 EBSD fields in pool boundary, centre and remelted zones; target ≥500–1000 indexed grains for robust size and texture statistics. | Report equivalent-circle diameter, aspect ratio, equiaxed area fraction, grain-boundary misorientation and texture index/MUD. Compare local modeled `(G,R)` with Hunt/KGT-type CET maps: `GR` controls cooling rate while `G/R` strongly influences morphology. Sc/Zr systems require nucleant density and undercooling terms; thermal criteria alone are not sufficient. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025) | Grain-size uncertainty is commonly 5–15% when several fields are pooled; equiaxed fraction approximately ±3–5 percentage points. Step sizes too large for the fine boundary zone systematically overestimate grain size and create false texture. | Lu et al., **10.3390/cryst13060913**; Michi et al., **10.1080/09506608.2021.1951580**; Cerri et al., **10.3390/cryst15010025** |
| 5 | Selective evaporation and composition drift—especially Mg, Zn, Li and brass Zn | Bulk powder and printed-pad/coupon chemistry by ICP-OES or ICP-MS after complete dissolution; EPMA/WDS for spatial maps; EDS only for screening; collect condensate/spatter where possible. Use multiple printed conditions spanning absorbed line energy and melting mode. | ASTM E3061 for ICP-AES analysis of Al alloys; laboratory digestion and certified-reference-material procedures | Preserve ≥5–10 g virgin powder for chemistry; print ≥3 pads/coupons at low, nominal and high energy. Digest ≥3 independent aliquots from powder and from each printed condition; sample the coupon interior rather than only oxidized surfaces. | Element loss: `L_i = (C_{i,powder}−C_{i,print})/C_{i,powder} ×100%`. Relate to absorbed line energy `A P/v`, not only nominal volumetric energy. Langmuir/Hertz–Knudsen flux: `J_i = α_i a_i p_i^{sat}(T)√[M_i/(2πRT)]`, integrated over melt surface area and lifetime; include gas shielding and activity. (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027) | ICP-OES commonly 1–3% relative for major elements and 3–10% near detection limits; sampling heterogeneity can dominate. SEM-EDS is generally unsuitable for detecting approximately 1% relative Mg loss. | Bärtl et al., **10.1007/s11665-022-06592-z**; Li et al., **10.1007/s11661-020-06073-9**; Mukherjee et al., **10.1038/s41524-024-01418-z** |
| 6 | Printability maps: LOF, balling, keyhole porosity, density and hot cracking | Stage 1: top-view microscopy/profilometry of single tracks. Stage 2: single-layer pads at several hatch spacings. Stage 3: small 5–10 mm cubes. Density by polished-section image analysis, Archimedes and preferably micro-CT for defect morphology. Crack density by stitched optical/SEM images and skeletonized line-length analysis. | ASTM B962 for Archimedes density; ASTM E3 for metallography; ASTM E1245 for automated image analysis; ASTM E1441 for CT guidance | Efficient design: 20–30 power–speed tracks, two replicates; 8–12 pads covering candidate window/hatch spacings; 6–12 confirmation cubes. Use randomized positions and include centre/edge locations. | LOF: `d<t` or failed overlap `(h/w)²+(t/d)²>1`; keyhole warning `d/w>0.5` plus rounded subsurface pores; balling commonly `L/w ≳2` and discontinuous track morphology. Relative density from images `ρ_rel = 1−A_pore/A_total`; crack density `CD = ΣL_crack/A`. Do not use `P/(vht)` as the sole map coordinate. (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034) | Optical area fraction: approximately ±0.05–0.2 percentage points for dense material if ≥3 large fields/planes are used; Archimedes often ±0.1–0.5% and can exceed 100% because of wetting, trapped gas or uncertain theoretical density. CT detection is voxel-size limited. Crack density commonly varies 10–30% between fields. | Sheikh et al., **10.1038/s41524-024-01436-x**; Zhang et al., **10.1108/RPJ-01-2021-0024**; Yang et al., **10.1016/j.addma.2021.102103** |
| 7 | Residual stress and stress-relief distortion | Laboratory XRD `sin²ψ` for near-surface stress; bridge/alligator or cantilever release measured by optical profilometry/DIC; incremental hole drilling with strain gauge or ESPI; contour method for larger cross-sections; neutron diffraction for through-thickness lattice strain. | EN 15305 for XRD residual stress; ASTM E837 for hole drilling; ISO 21432 for neutron diffraction | XRD: ≥3 nominally identical coupons and several positions/directions. Bridge/cantilever: ≥3 repeats per condition and pre/post-release geometry. Contour and neutron methods usually require coupons thicker/larger than desktop calibration specimens. | `ε_φψ = (d_φψ−d₀)/d₀`; for biaxial stress, stress follows the slope of `d` or `2θ` versus `sin²ψ` using appropriate X-ray elastic constants. Cantilever/bridge distortion is compared directly with thermo-mechanical FE predictions; simple beam-curvature conversion is valid only when geometry and eigenstrain assumptions are satisfied. (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000041) | XRD is often ±20–50 MPa under favourable conditions but texture, coarse grains and uncertain stress-free `d₀` can dominate in Al/Cu. Hole drilling is commonly ±5–15%; release geometries show approximately 5–10% repeatability. Neutron uncertainty is often tens of MPa and spatial resolution is millimetric. | Representative LPBF methods summarized by Bertoli et al.; XRD/hole-drilling implementation evidence in (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036); released-cantilever/DIC example in (pqac-00000041) |

Keep field of view several millimetres above and behind the pool; record no-laser background and spatial calibration. | Particle velocity `u = Δs/Δt`; kinetic energy `E_k = ½m u²` using equivalent-sphere mass; report event rate per track length/time, ejection-angle distribution and denuded width. In Al, Mg/Zn evaporation, oxide films and low density increase sensitivity to plume-driven entrainment and oxidized redeposition. (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055) | Position is typically ±1–2 pixels; velocity about ±5–15% when particles persist for several frames. Particle mass/kinetic energy may be uncertain by >30% because diameter and temperature are poorly known. Schlieren is primarily qualitative unless carefully calibrated. | Guo et al., **10.1088/2631-7990/ad4e1d**; Li et al., **10.3390/mi13081366**; Liu et al., **10.3390/mi14071351**; Rehman et al., **10.3390/met11122023** |
| 9 | Powder PSD, morphology, flowability, packing density, O/H and moisture | Laser diffraction for volume PSD; dynamic image analysis/SEM for number PSD, satellites and shape; Hall/Carney funnel; rotating-drum avalanche or GranuDrum/Revolution analyzer; FT4 dynamic, aeration, permeability and shear tests; apparent/tap density; He pycnometry; LECO-type inert-gas-fusion O/N/H analyzer; Karl Fischer or controlled loss-on-drying/TGA for moisture. | ISO 13320; ISO 13322; ISO/ASTM 52907; ASTM B213 Hall; ASTM B964 Carney; ASTM B212 apparent density; ASTM B527 tap density; ASTM E1019 for O/N/H in applicable alloys; ASTM E1447 for H in Ti-based materials—not a universal Al/Cu method | Use representative riffled samples. Laser diffraction typically needs <1 g per repeat; imaging ≥10,000 particles; funnel tests commonly 50 g and may be unsuitable for cohesive Al powder; FT4 often 10–25 mL; chemistry approximately 0.1–1 g per replicate. Perform ≥3 repeats and retain an unopened baseline sample. | Report `D10/D50/D90`, span `(D90−D10)/D50`, circularity/sphericity, apparent and tap density. Hausner ratio `HR=ρ_tap/ρ_bulk`; Carr index `CI=100(ρ_tap−ρ_bulk)/ρ_tap`. Flow time alone does not predict spreadability; combine PSD/morphology, dynamic flow and a recoated-layer image or mass-per-area test. (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049) | Laser-diffraction repeatability is commonly 1–3% but assumes an optical model and near-spherical particles; image-analysis bias depends on segmentation and sampling. ### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Priority rank | Measurement | What it calibrates or validates | Minimum specimen count and estimated powder use | Notes |
|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Powder PSD, morphology, flow, packing, and chemistry | Powder-bed packing fraction, density, effective conductivity, initial alloy composition, and spreading reproducibility | Three riffled aliquots; 1–3 g for laser diffraction, 2–5 g for imaging, 30–50 g reusable for funnel testing or 10–25 mL reusable for rheometry, and 1–3 g for O/H and chemistry. Net irreversible use: about 5–10 g. | Record D10, D50, D90, morphology, apparent and tap density, O/H, moisture, and ICP-OES chemistry. For cohesive Al powder, supplement funnel tests with dynamic flow and recoated-layer mass per area. Retain an unopened baseline aliquot. (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049) |
| 2 | Single-track top views and transverse and longitudinal melt-pool sections | Effective absorptivity and beam-radius calibration; width, depth, and length validation; conduction-to-keyhole boundary | Twenty to thirty power–speed conditions, two tracks per condition, at least three transverse sections per track, five near transition or keyhole, and selected longitudinal sections. About 5–15 g circulated; less than 1 g fused. | Include bare-plate and powder-layer tracks if possible. Measure the beam independently, fit absorptivity primarily to depth and width, and reserve 20–30% of conditions for validation. A depth-to-width ratio above about 0.5 warns of keyholing. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015) |
| 3 | Single-layer pad topography, continuity, overlap, and area porosity | Hatch-spacing and remelting calibration; transfer from isolated tracks to interacting tracks; LOF and balling boundaries | Eight to twelve pads of about 5 × 5 or 10 × 10 mm, using two or three hatch spacings. About 10–25 g circulated and 2–5 g fused. | Measure uncovered area, continuity, roughness, and overlap by optical mosaics or profilometry. Test the geometric overlap criterion but confirm it experimentally because conduction models omit melt flow, oxide films, and packing variability. (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033) |
| 4 | Small-cube or short-coupon density and pore morphology | Multilayer heat-accumulation and printability validation; separation of LOF from keyhole porosity | Six to twelve coupons, preferably 5 × 5 × 5 mm, including three repeats at the nominal condition and several boundary conditions. About 10–35 g fused and 30–80 g circulated. | Analyze at least three polished planes per condition. Use Archimedes as a secondary check; use micro-CT on two or three coupons to distinguish irregular LOF pores from rounded keyhole pores. (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000034) |
| 5 | Cellular or dendritic spacing across melt pools | Modeled cooling rate and spatial thermal-history validation after melt-pool calibration | Reuse sections from at least three low-, nominal-, and high-energy tracks or coupons; measure at least 100 cells or intercepts in pool-boundary, center, and trailing regions. No additional powder. | Establish or validate an alloy-specific spacing–cooling-rate relation. Do not import constants uncritically from cast Al-Si or another alloy. Estimate local solidification rate from scan speed and the measured interface orientation. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020) |
| 6 | ICP-OES of virgin powder and low-, nominal-, and high-energy printed material | Selective-evaporation validation and the actual chemistry used for CALPHAD and thermophysical calculations | Three independent powder aliquots and three printed conditions, preferably with triplicate digestions. About 2–5 g of powder and 3–10 g of printed material consumed. | Sample coupon interiors. Report relative Mg, Zn, or Li loss and relate it to absorbed line energy and melt mode rather than nominal volumetric energy alone. Use EPMA/WDS for spatial segregation; EDS is generally inadequate for small bulk losses. (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027) |
| 7 | EBSD grain size, texture, and columnar-to-equiaxed transition | Validation of derived thermal-gradient and solidification-rate fields and Hunt/KGT-type CET predictions | Reuse one nominal pad or coupon and one contrasting condition; map at least three complete melt pools and at least 500–1000 indexed grains. No additional powder. | Combine coarse whole-pool maps with 0.05–0.2 µm step-size maps at pool boundaries and centers. Report equiaxed fraction, grain size, aspect ratio, misorientation, and texture intensity. Sc/Zr systems also require nucleant-density considerations. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025) |
| 8 | XRD sin²ψ residual stress or released-cantilever deflection | Downstream thermo-mechanical stress and distortion validation; little direct leverage on melt-pool heat-source calibration | Three coupons or cantilevers at the selected condition. About 5–20 g fused; specimens can subsequently be reused for metallography. | Measure both in-plane directions at several positions and use appropriate X-ray elastic constants. For small Al coupons, release distortion may be more repeatable than absolute XRD because texture, weak diffraction, and uncertain stress-free spacing can dominate. (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000041) |
| 9 | High-speed spatter and plume imaging, optionally with schlieren | Diagnosis of absorptivity transitions, vapor recoil, denudation, and unstable keyholing; optional for conduction-model calibration | Image at least three tracks in conduction, transition, and keyhole regimes while reusing the track matrix. Additional fused powder is negligible; about 2–5 g circulated. | Use at least 5–20 kfps for event counts and plume shape and preferably 50–100 kfps for droplet dynamics. Particularly useful for Mg- or Zn-bearing Al alloys, where evaporation may invalidate constant-absorptivity assumptions. (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000055) |
| — | Integrated minimum campaign | Sufficient independent data to calibrate a conduction heat source and validate multilayer printability without excessive fitting | About 25 track conditions, eight pads, and six to nine cubes or coupons. Target 40–80 g fused or consumed and 100–180 g maximum circulated, leaving reserve material from a 100–300 g lot. | Proceed sequentially: powder baseline, tracks, heat-source fit, pads, cubes, then microstructure and chemistry. Sieve reusable powder and retain virgin powder for comparisons. Defer EBSD, stress, and plume work until geometry and density meet predefined validation limits. |

info.name: view_images
info.description:
Retrieve images from a document.

Use this tool when you need to see figures, tables, or other visual content.
The tool works by asking a weaker LLM agent to scan through the document, looking for
visual content matching the query you provide. When the agent finds matches, it will
crop the page to the relevant region. It can be tasked to return multiple images,
if desired. Note that the weaker LLM may be worse at *understanding* images than
you, so double-check its conclusions about the returned images. It is also stateless,
i.e. it will not remember what you have asked it to find in the past.

Use this tool carefully. It is difficult to retrieve images, and the images
themselves will fill up your context window quickly. Here are some guidelines:
1. ALWAYS use this tool if the question explicitly mentions 'Table X' or 'Figure Y'.
   These questions require visual content and cannot be answered with text alone.
2. Use this tool as a fallback when gather_evidence fails repeatedly (2+ times
   returning 'No relevant evidence'). This suggests the answer may be in visual content.
3. When gather_evidence returns text mentioning 'see Figure X' or 'shown in Table Y',
   you should call this tool to examine that specific visual reference.
4. Only call this tool after directly inspecting relevant text with read_text
   to confirm the document likely contains the visual you need.
5. Don't use this tool in a broad-spectrum way (don't call on many documents
   just to see what might be relevant).
6. Never call this tool in parallel with itself.
7. Users like visual evidence, so call this tool at least once before answering so you
   can provide some image citations in the answer. Add this to your plan so you do not forget.
   For images to be presented to the user, they must be cited in the final answer after retrieval
   by this tool. You may ignore this instruction if the request is for the question is asking
   for a specific piece of information and is not an open-ended research question.
8. NEVER cite full-page images in your final answer, unless they are full-page panels figures or
   tables. Cite relevant cropped regions if available, otherwise consider calling this tool again
   to find a smaller region that answers the query.

query.description:
Query to search for visual content in the document. If you know the specific
figure/table/formula you are looking for, you can specify it here (e.g. "find me
Figure 3" or "extract the table on page 10"). You can also request based on content
(e.g. "find me all volcano plots of gene X" or "I need the formula for the growth rate").
You can even include explicit instructions for the LLM agent to follow (if helpful, not
necessarily required). The more specific and clear your query is here, the higher the
chance of success.

info.name: patent_search
info.description:
Search for patents to increase the patent count.

Repeat previous calls with the same query to continue a search.
Only repeat a maximum of three times.
This tool can be called concurrently.
This tool introduces novel patents, so invoke it when just beginning
or when unsatisfied with the current evidence.

query.description:
A search query for patents (using Google Patents). Never include temporal
filters here (e.g. specific years or dates); instead use the `after` and `before`
arguments. Never include author filters here; instead use the `inventor` argument.
Supports the following syntax, but they can be brittle and are not preferred; try
simple queries where possible:
- Boolean operators: AND (default), OR, and - (NOT)
- Exact phrases: "quoted text"
- Proximity: NEAR/x, ADJ/x (ordered), WITH (20 words), SAME (200 words)
- Field search: TI=(title), AB=(abstract), CL=(claims)
- CPC codes: cpc:A01B or CPC=B60R22/low (includes children)
- Wildcards: ? (0-1 char), * (0+ chars), # (exactly 1 char)
- Chemistry: exact molecule names, SSS=molecule (substructure),
  ~molecule (similar), SMILES strings, SMARTS=pattern, InChI keys,
  CL=~molecule (chemistry in claims)

info.name: create_artifact
info.description:
Create an artifact that can be used in the final answer, based on information
you have collected so far.

How it works: the full message history thus far is passed to another LLM,
along with the question and your description. The LLM is tasked to create
an artifact that matches your specifications, including a title, caption,
and markdown content. You drive the process by specifying the type and
describing what you want.

Only use this tool *after* you have gathered sufficient evidence or
information to create a new artifact. Do not call this tool in parallel
with tools that are searching for information or evidence that would be
necessary to create this artifact.

It is very helpful after calls to several search tools,
after calls to the `gather_evidence` tool, but it is not required.
However, it should be called before the `answer` tool at
least one time, but more may be given if specifically helpful for
the task, so that the `answer` tool can use the artifacts for the answer.

An artifact can be any string representable fact or list of facts,
formatted using markdown syntax. The artifact will be generated as one of
the following types:
- table: Markdown tables with rows and columns (e.g., findings, methods, molecules)
- code_block: Code snippets in fenced code blocks
- blockquote: Quoted text or important facts (using > prefix)
- image: AI-generated image (chart, diagram, or visualization)

Each artifact consists of:
- A short title (3-8 words) that names what the artifact contains
- A caption (1-2 sentences) describing what the artifact shows and why it's useful
- Markdown content in a single element type (validated automatically with retries if needed)
  For image type, content is a markdown image embed ``![title](data:image/png;base64,...)``,
  embedding the PNG directly as a base64 data URL.

artifact_type.description:
Artifact type to create. Must be one of: table,
code_block, blockquote, image.
artifact_type.title: Artifact Type

description.description:
Description of what you want in the artifact. Be specific
about what information should be included, how it should be organized,
and what columns/sections/content you want. This guides the summary LLM.
For image type, describe the visual you want generated in detail.
description.title: Description

info.name: read_text
info.description:
Given a list of text names, read their contents.

This tool is valuable to read the full contents of specific parts of documents,
complementing the `gather_evidence` tool's indirect approach.
This can be an especially useful tool if `gather_evidence` does not find evidence,
but you think it is very likely that specific documents are still relevant to the question.

A list of up to 10 text names to read.
These text names can be any valid text names retrieved by other tools.

info.name: clinical_trials_search
info.description:
Search for clinical trials, with support for repeated calls and concurrent execution.

Will add new clinical trials to the state, and return metadata about the number of trials found.

query.description:
The search query string. Supports complex boolean expressions, field-specific
searches, and query modifiers through operators. All configuration is done through
operators in the query string.
Query Syntax:
    Basic Search:
        Simple text automatically uses default EXPANSION[Relaxation] and COVERAGE[Contains]
        >>> "heart attack"

    Modified Search:
        Use operators to modify search behavior:
        >>> 'EXPANSION[None]COVERAGE[FullMatch]"exact phrase"'
        >>> 'EXPANSION[Concept]heart attack'

    Field Search:
        Specify fields using AREA operator:
        >>> 'AREA[InterventionName]aspirin'
        >>> 'AREA[Phase]PHASE3'

    Location Search:
        Use SEARCH operator for compound location queries:
        >>> 'cancer AND SEARCH[Location](AREA[LocationCity]Boston AND AREA[LocationState]Massachusetts)'

    Complex Boolean:
        Combine terms with AND, OR, NOT and parentheses:
        >>> '(cancer OR tumor) AND NOT (EXPANSION[None]pediatric OR AREA[StdAge]CHILD)'

    Date Ranges:
        Use RANGE to specify date ranges with formats like "yyyy-MM" or "yyyy-MM-dd".
        Note that MIN and MAX can be used for open-ended ranges:
        >>> AREA[ResultsFirstPostDate]RANGE[2015-01-01, MAX]

Operators:
    EXPANSION[type]: Controls term expansion
        - None: Exact match only, case and accent sensitive
        - Term: Includes lexical variants (plurals, spellings)
        - Concept: Includes UMLS synonyms
        - Relaxation: Relaxes adjacency requirements (default)
        - Lossy: Allows missing partial terms

    COVERAGE[type]: Controls text matching
        - FullMatch: Must match entire field
        - StartsWith: Must match beginning of field
        - EndsWith: Must match end of field
        - Contains: Must match part of field (default)

    AREA[field]: Specifies field to search
        - See Field Reference for available fields

    SEARCH[type]: Groups field searches
        - Location: Groups location-related fields
        - Study: Groups study-related fields

Usage Notes:
    - All search expressions are implicitly OR expressions
    - Operator precedence (highest to lowest): terms/source operators, NOT/context operators, AND, OR
    - Use quotes for exact phrase matching: "heart attack"
    - Use parentheses for grouping: (heart OR cardiac) AND attack
    - Use backslash to escape operators: \AND
    - Default expansion is EXPANSION[Relaxation]
    - Default coverage is COVERAGE[Contains]

info.name: gather_evidence
info.description:
Given a specific question, gather evidence from full-text of documents that have been retrieved by
previous tool calls.

Here is how the tool works: the provided question is posed to all texts retrieved thus far
by other tools. An LLM sees each text independently and is prompted to find information relevant
to the question.

That is, we sample evidence `e \sim LLM(prompt, text, q)` for each text. We only return pieces of
evidence `e` that are sufficiently relevant to the question; if the text is irrelevant, then `e`
is not included in the final response of this tool. Note that this LLM does not see the conversation
history thus far, only the question and each text. Note that it only sees text, no images or other
media from the contents (though tables and formulae may be parseable in some cases).

Think of this tool as an efficient way to deeply scan all retrieved documents for evidence. It
is complementary to the `read_text` tool, which can be used to directly inspect a subset of the
retrieved documents.

A valuable time to invoke this tool is after another tool finds potentially relevant documents.
Feel free to invoke this tool in parallel with other tools, but do not call this tool in parallel with itself.
Only invoke this tool when the document count is above zero, or this tool will be useless.

If you call this tool 2+ times and repeatedly get 'No relevant evidence found',
consider whether the answer might be in visual content (figures/tables) rather than text,
and use appropriate tools if available to access that content.

Once you receive evidence from this tool:

1. Read Carefully: Don't skim. The evidence may contain multiple similar terms
   or values—make sure you identify the RIGHT one.

2. For Comparative Questions: If the question asks "which X has greatest Y",
   check that the evidence includes information about ALL relevant X options, not
   just one or two. If you only see partial information, gather more evidence.

3. Check for Noise: Verify that numbers or terms aren't just metadata
   (page numbers, reference IDs, dates). Look for the value in meaningful
   scientific context.

4. Context Matters: A term appearing 71 times doesn't mean it's always the answer.
   Verify which occurrence actually answers the question asked.

If the evidence doesn't clearly answer the question, gather more evidence before
concluding. Don't guess based on partial information.

info.name: create_plan
info.description:
Create a plan to construct a thorough and accurate answer.

Decompose the input task into a set of sub-objectives that need to
be met in order to form the answer. Subsequently, when working on solving
the query, you can focus on these objectives one by one. Note that the
`update_plan` tool allows you to change the objectives if needed.

In addition to the objectives you deem necessary, add one final objective
to call the `answer` tool with your final answer, so that you do not
forget to submit your answer.

plan_json.description:
A JSON string encoding an object with an "objectives" list;
never pass objectives separately.
Each objective should be a dictionary with the following keys:
- "id": (int) an integer id for the plan objective
- "objective": (str) a human readable description of the objective's goal
- "rationale": (str) a human readable rationale
    describing why this objective is necessary and appropriate for the query.
- "status": (str) updated task status, default to pending,

    "pending" is yet to be started,
    "in-progress" is the current objective being solved,
    "completed" is successfully completed with acceptance criteria met.
- "result": (str|None) The result of the objective, default to None.
- "evaluation": (str|None) Description of why the objective result
    meets the criteria for being complete. Default to None.

info.name: answer
info.description:
Submit your final answer to the user. You MUST call this tool on your final answer.
If you mark all objectives as completed but have not yet called this tool, then
the answer will not be submitted. Note that this tool should only be called once, as it
immediately terminates the run and submits the answer.

Write an answer based on the evidence from gather_evidence results in message history.
If the context provides insufficient information, provide a partial answer and explain
why it is partial (e.g. the question is currently an open question in the field,
you were unable to obtain certain papers, etc.).

For each part of your answer, indicate which sources most support it via citation IDs at
the end of sentences, like (pqac-0000ABCD).
You are only allowed to cite available context IDs, indicated in previous messages by "Context IDs that may be cited:".
## Valid citation examples, only use comma/space delimited parentheticals:

- (pqac-0000ABCD, pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000IJKL)

## Invalid citation examples:

- (pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD;pqac-0000EFGH)
- (pqac-0000ABCD-pqac-0000EFGH)
- pqac-0000ABCD and pqac-0000EFGH
- Example's work pqac-0000ABCD
- (pages pqac-0000ABCD)
- ![description](pqac-0000ABCD)
- ()

Do not concatenate citation ids, just use them as-is.

When writing your answer, embed artifacts if relevant artifacts have been previously
created by the `create_artifact` tool. To embed an artifact, simply include this in your
answer, on its own line and without any additional formatting (i.e. no backticks, code fences,
quotes, additional tags, etc.).
Always provide at least some introductory sentence or paragraph before referring to an artifact,
so that the artifact is properly contextualized.
Here is an example reference to an artifact with ID "artifact-XY":
<artifact id="artifact-XY"/>

Valid artifact IDs are indicated in previous messages by 'Artifact IDs that may be injected into the answer:'.


Double-check your answer:

1. Evidence Match: Re-read the specific evidence snippets you're citing. Does your
   answer actually match what they say? Don't rely on memory from 20+ messages ago.

2. For Comparative Questions ("which X has greatest/maximum/highest Y"):
   - Did you examine ALL options mentioned in the evidence?
   - Did you explicitly compare their values?
   - Example: If evidence mentions "Pancreatic: 0.92, Liver: 0.85, Lung: 0.78",
     verify you compared all three, not just two.

3. For Specific Value Questions ("How many", "What is the", specific terms):
   - Does the exact value you're stating appear in the evidence?
   - Are you extracting from the right context (not noise like page numbers)?

4. Sanity Check: Read your answer. Does it directly address what was asked?

Don't use Markdown image syntax like ![...](...) to reference media in your answer,
because media get automatically linked by the system based on your answer's citations.

Write in the style of a scientific article, with concise sentences and
coherent paragraphs. This answer will be used directly,
so do not add any extraneous information.

messages.content:
Use the tools to answer the question: We want to measure, for new aluminium alloys (and some copper alloys) printed by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), the quantities that the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing Module and similar melt-pool models predict, so we can calibrate and validate them. Our printing is small-scale: single tracks, single-layer pads, and small cubes/coupons (desktop LPBF with a 200-500 W, 1070 nm fiber laser, ~50-100 um spot; plus an Aconity MIDI and a Concept Laser M2 elsewhere). Alloys: AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc-Zr (Scalmalloy-type), lean Al-Mg-Zr, Al-Mn, Al-Ce and Al-Cu alloys, and Cu alloys (Ni-Al bronze, Cu-Ni). Please review the peer-reviewed literature and, for each item below, give the measurement method(s), typical equipment, sample preparation, how many tracks/samples are needed, the analysis (with equations), the open-source code available, typical uncertainties, and published examples with DOIs (prefer Al and Cu alloys):

1. Melt pool width, depth and length from single-track cross-sections and top-view imaging: etchants for Al and Cu alloys, number of sections per track, conduction vs transition vs keyhole mode classification (depth/width ratio, normalized enthalpy deltaH/h_s from King et al., keyhole number / Ke from Gan et al.), and heat-source calibration (absorptivity, beam radius, Goldak/Gaussian parameters) against measured melt pools, including how the Thermo-Calc AM Module, Eagar-Tsai / Rosenthal models and FLOW-3D type CFD have been calibrated.
2. Laser absorptivity of Al and Cu powder beds and bulk at ~1070 nm: integrating-sphere and calorimetric methods (e.g., Trapp et al. LLNL, NIST integrating-sphere work), values vs power/speed/mode.
3. Thermal history, peak temperature, thermal gradient G and solidification rate R: thermocouples, two-colour pyrometry, IR thermography, and post-mortem proxies (cell/dendrite arm spacing vs cooling rate relations for Al-Si and Al-Mg alloys, R = v cos(theta) from melt-pool shape), and in-situ synchrotron X-ray imaging/diffraction (e.g., Advanced Photon Source 32-ID) measurements of melt pool, keyhole and solidification.
4. Columnar-to-equiaxed transition, grain size and texture in LPBF Al alloys (Sc/Zr inoculation): EBSD on tracks and pads, comparison with G-R maps and Hunt/KGT-type CET models.
5. Composition change by selective evaporation (Mg, Zn, Li loss in Al alloys; Zn in brasses): ICP-OES/EDS/EPMA of powder vs printed material, measured Mg loss vs energy density, comparison with evaporation models.
6. Printability maps: lack of fusion, keyholing, balling and hot cracking criteria; density (Archimedes, CT, optical image analysis) vs process parameters; keyhole porosity thresholds; crack density measurement; how to build printability maps from single tracks and pads with minimal powder.
7. Residual stress in small LPBF coupons: XRD sin^2(psi), bridge-curvature / cantilever deflection, contour method, hole drilling, neutron diffraction.
8. Spatter and vapour plume: high-speed imaging and schlieren, and their relevance for Al.
9. Powder properties that control LPBF of these alloys: particle size distribution (laser diffraction vs image analysis, ISO 13322 / ISO 13320), flowability (Hall/Carney, revolution powder analysis, FT4, avalanche/GranuDrum), apparent/tap density, oxygen and hydrogen content (inert gas fusion, ASTM E1019 / E1447), moisture.

End with a ranked list of the minimum set of single-track, pad and coupon measurements that best calibrates the AM module (or open alternatives) for a new Al alloy with only ~100-300 g of powder, and give a full reference list with DOIs.


Start by making a plan, and update the plan as you go. Your answer will be returned to the user when all plan objectives are completed. Be thorough and ensure your evidence matches the user's question.
I'll create a comprehensive plan to address this multi-faceted question about characterization methods for LPBF-printed aluminum and copper alloys.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) attracts the attention of high-end manufacturing sectors for its capability of depositing free-form components with elevated mechanical properties. However, due to the intrinsic nature of the feedstock material and the interaction with the laser beam, the process is prone to defect formation and manufacturing inaccuracies. Therefore, the development of a monitoring architecture capable of measuring the geometrical features of the process tool (i.e., the melt pool generated by the laser-material interaction) is of paramount importance. This information may then be exploited to evaluate process stability. In this work, a high-speed camera was implemented coaxially in the optical chain of an LPBF system to extrapolate the geometrical features of the molten pool surface and its oscillatory behaviour, with elevated spatial and temporal resolution. A secondary light source was tested in both coaxial and off-axis configuration to dominate process emission and assess optimal illumination conditions for extracting the molten pool’s geometrical features. Preliminary results showed that the off-axis configuration of the illumination light enabled direct measurement of the molten pool surface geometry. A newly developed image processing algorithm based on illuminated images obtained via the coaxial observation frame was employed to provide automated identification of the melt pool geometry. Moreover, bright reflections of the external illumination over the melt surface could be clearly observed and used to characterise the oscillatory motion of the molten material. This information may therefore be taken as an indirect indicator of the molten pool penetration depth, hence providing information regarding the subsurface geometry. A successive experimental investigation showed the capability of the monitoring architecture to resolve the molten pool’s length, width and area with elevated acquisition frequency. Molten pool surface oscillations in the kHz range could be correlated to the penetration depth while the molten pool width measured via the high-speed imaging setup corresponded to the track width of the depositions. Hence, the methodological approach for the concurrent measurement of the molten pool’s geometry in three spatial dimensions was demonstrated and may be used to track the stability of LPBF depositions.

Abstract:
The integrative potential of LPBF-printed parts for various innovative applications depends upon the robustness and infallibility of the part quality. Eliminating or sufficiently reducing factors contributing to the formation of defects is an integral step to achieving satisfiable part quality. Significant research efforts have been conducted to understand and quantify the triggers and origins of LPBF defects by investigating the material properties and process parameters for LPBF-printed geometries using various sensing technologies and techniques. Frequently, combinations of sensing techniques are applied to deepen the understanding of the investigated phenomena. The main objectives of this review are to cover the roles of selective sensing technologies by (1) providing a summary of LPBF metal print defects and their corresponding causes, (2) informing readers of the vast number and types of technologies and methodologies available to detect defects in LPBF-printed parts, and (3) equipping readers with publications geared towards defect detection using combinations of sensing technologies. Due to the large pool of developed sensing technology in the last few years for LPBF-printed parts that may be designed for targeting a specific defect in metal alloys, the article herein focuses on sensing technology that is common and applicable to most common defects and has been utilized in characterization for an extended period with proven efficiency and applicability to LPBF metal parts defect detection.

Abstract:
High-irradiance lasers incident on metal surfaces create a complex, dynamic process through which the metal can rapidly change from highly reflective to strongly absorbing. Absolute knowledge of this process underpins important industrial laser processes such as laser welding, cutting, and metal additive manufacturing. Determining the time-dependent absorptance of the laser light by a material is important, not only for gaining a fundamental understanding of the light-matter interaction but also for improving process design in manufacturing. Measurements of the dynamic optical absorptance are notoriously difficult due to the rapidly changing nature of the absorbing medium. These data are also of vital importance to process modelers, whose complex simulations need reliable, accurate input data; yet, there are very few available. In this work, we measure the time-dependent, reflected light during a 10-ms laser spot weld using an integrating-sphere apparatus. From this, we calculate the dynamic absorptance for 1070-nm-wavelength light incident on 316L stainless steel. The time resolution of our experiment (less than 1 μs) allows the determination of the precise conditions under which several important physical phenomena occur, such as melt and keyhole formation. The average absorptances determined optically are compared with calorimetrically determined values, and it is found that the calorimeter severely underestimates the absorbed energy due to mass lost during the spot weld. Weld-nugget cross sections are also presented to verify our interpretation of the optical results, as well as to provide experimental data for weld-model validation.

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
        <jats:p>The quantification of absorbed light is essential for understanding laser-material interactions and melt pool dynamics in order to minimize defects in additively manufactured metal components. The geometry of a vapor depression, also known as a keyhole, in melt pools formed during laser melting is closely related to laser energy absorption. This relationship has been observed by the state-of-the-art in situ high speed synchrotron x-ray visualization and integrating sphere radiometry. These two techniques create a temporally resolved dataset consisting of keyhole images and corresponding laser absorptance. In this work, we propose two different approaches to predict laser absorptance. The end-to-end approach uses deep convolutional neural networks to learn features of unprocessed x-ray images automatically without human supervision and predict the laser energy absorptance. The two-stage approach uses a semantic segmentation model to engineer geometric features and predict absorptance using classical regression models. Though with different advantages, both approaches reached a smooth mean absolute error less than 3.4%.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>A low magnetic Zr-1Mo alloy was fabricated by a powder bed fusion (PBF) process using a fiber laser. The microstructure, surface morphology, and pore distribution of the as-built Zr-1Mo alloy were observed. Its magnetic susceptibility and Vickers hardness were evaluated by magnetic susceptibility balance and a microindentation tester, respectively. The as-built Zr-1Mo alloy mainly consisted of an α′ phase with an acicular structure. From the processing maps of the surface morphology and pore distribution, open pores on the top surface due to the lack of fusion corresponded to grid-like distributed pores, and large pores corresponded to balling particles on the top surface. The Vickers hardness was influenced by the oxygen and nitrogen contents rather than the porosity. The magnetic susceptibilities of the as-built Zr-1Mo alloy still were one-third those of Ti-6Al-4V and Ti-6Al-7Nb, thus PBF can be applicable to the fabrication process for the low magnetic Zr-1Mo alloy.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Keyhole porosity is a key concern in laser powder-bed fusion (LPBF), potentially impacting component fatigue life. However, some keyhole porosity formation mechanisms, e.g., keyhole fluctuation, collapse and bubble growth and shrinkage, remain unclear. Using synchrotron X-ray imaging we reveal keyhole and bubble behaviour, quantifying their formation dynamics. The findings support the hypotheses that: (i) keyhole porosity can initiate not only in unstable, but also in the transition keyhole regimes created by high laser power-velocity conditions, causing fast radial keyhole fluctuations (2.5–10 kHz); (ii) transition regime collapse tends to occur part way up the rear-wall; and (iii) immediately after keyhole collapse, bubbles undergo rapid growth due to pressure equilibration, then shrink due to metal-vapour condensation. Concurrent with condensation, hydrogen diffusion into the bubble slows the shrinkage and stabilises the bubble size. The keyhole fluctuation and bubble evolution mechanisms revealed here may guide the development of control systems for minimising porosity. Understanding the keyhole porosity formation is important in laser powder bed fusion. Here the authors reveal the dynamics of keyhole fluctuation, and collapse that induces bubble formation with three main stages of evolution; growth, shrinkage, and being captured by the solidification front.

Abstract:
In the metal additive manufacturing (AM) process of laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), there are a limited number of materials suitable for producing parts with high density and desired mechanical properties. To establish novel materials, it is essential to determine optimized process parameters in order to overcome process-related challenges and mitigate defects such as lack of fusion, keyholing, and balling. Scaling laws based on thermophysical properties and process parameters can be used to transfer knowledge from other materials or LPBF systems. In this work, a scaling law is used to adjust process parameters for single-track experiments over a wide range, which are laser power P _L (100–1000 W), scan speed v _s (300–2500 mm/s), and laser spot size d _s (0.08–0.25 mm). Compared to existing studies, the parameter range is thus extended towards large laser spot sizes and high laser powers. The scaling law used is based on the calculation of the normalized enthalpy $$\frac{\Delta H}{{h}_{s}}$$ Δ H h s . The ratio of the deposited energy density $$\Delta$$ Δ H and the melting enthalpy h _s correlates with the dimensions of the melt pool. According to the aspect ratio $${\delta }_{\mathrm{c}}$$ δ c of the melt pool of each single track, the respective melting mode—conduction, transition, and keyhole mode—was identified. The process parameters of the single tracks in transition mode were used to optimize the density of the LPBF specimens with varying hatch distance h _d (0.06–0.12 mm), resulting in specimens with a relative density of > 99.8%. The proposed methodology can accelerate the process parameter finding for new alloys and avoid process-related defects. Graphical Abstract

Abstract:
In situ optical absorptivity measurements are carried out to clarify the physics of the laser‐material interactions involved and to validate both finite element and analytical models describing laser powder bed fusion processing. Absorption of laser energy is evaluated directly using precise calorimetry measurements and compared to melt pool depths for common structural metal alloys (Ti‐6Al‐4V, Inconel 625, and stainless steel 316L) as a function of incident laser power, scan velocity and laser beam diameter. Changes in both absorptivity and melt pool depths for all materials are found to vary strongly across the conduction‐keyhole mode threshold. A hydrodynamic finite element model is coupled to a ray‐tracing‐based absorptivity model, yielding excellent agreement with the experimental results and elucidating additional physics. The experimental results are further analyzed using normalized enthalpy (β) and normalized thermal diffusion length (L*th) relations and demonstrate that the normalized melt pool depth (d* = d/a, where d is melt pool depth and a is beam radius) is proportional to βL*th, while absorptivity follows an asymptotic exponential function against βL*th. Expressions for melt pool depth and laser absorptivity across different materials and laser scan systems are derived and thus provide useful tools to accelerate the optimization of laser processing parameters for metal 3D printing processes.

Abstract:
Research on powder-based additive manufacturing of aluminium alloys is rapidly increasing, and recent breakthroughs in printing of defect-free parts promise substantial movement beyond traditional Al–Si–Mg) systems. One potential technological advantage of aluminium additive manufacturing, however, has received little attention: the design of alloys for use at T > ∼200°C, or ∼1/2 of the absolute melting temperature of aluminium. Besides offering lightweighting and improved energy efficiency through replacement of ferrous, titanium, and nickel-based alloys at 200–450°C, development of such alloys will reduce economic roadblocks for widespread implementation of aluminium additive manufacturing. We herein review the existing additive manufacturing literature for three categories of potential high-temperature alloys, discuss strategies for optimizing microstructures for elevated-temperature performance, and highlight gaps in current research. Although extensive microstructural characterisation has been performed on these alloys, we conclude that evaluations of their high-temperature mechanical properties and corrosion responses are severely deficient.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is a typical additive manufacturing technology that offers significant advantages in the production of complex components. With the rapid heating and cooling characteristics of LPBF, a large amount of solid solution of alloying elements in the matrix can be achieved to form supersaturated solid solutions, thus enhancing the properties of LPBF alloys. For the unique microstructure, the heat treatment process needs to be adjusted accordingly. In this work, a Zr/Sc-modified Al-Mg alloy processed by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) with relatively low cost and good mechanical properties was investigated. The fine microstructure was obtained under rapid solidification conditions. The nanoscale Al3(Sc,Zr) particles precipitated at the molten pool boundary during solidification. These particles, as effective heterogeneous nucleators, further refined the α-Al grains and improved the mechanical properties of the alloy. As a result, the alloy exhibited a heterogeneous microstructure consisting of columnar grains in the center of the molten pool and equiaxed grains at the boundaries. The rapid solidification resulted in the supersaturation of solute atoms in the α-Al matrix, which significantly enhanced the solid solution strengthening effect. With the LPBF processing parameters of a combination of a laser power of 250 W, a laser scanning speed of 833 mm/s, and stripe scanning mode, the tensile strength of the alloy reached 401.4 ± 5.7 MPa, which was significantly higher than that of the cast alloys with aging treatment (281.1 ± 1.3 MPa). The heat treatment promoted the formation of secondary Al3(Sc,Zr), Mn/Mg-rich phases. The ultimate tensile strength and elongation at fracture after aging at 325 °C for 2 h were 536.0 ± 1.7 MPa and 14.8 ± 0.8%, respectively. The results provide insight into the preparation of aluminum alloys with relatively low cost and excellent mechanical properties.

Abstract:
Scalmalloy® is an Al-Mg-Sc-Zr alloy designed for the additive manufacturing of components used in various industrial applications. It is primarily used in aerospace and automotive fields due to its low density and high strength. The present brief review aims to outline the state-of-the-art heat treatments currently applied on the as-built Scalmalloy®. The as-built alloy shows yield strength values of 256–278 MPa, ultimate tensile strength of 349–350 MPa, and elongation of 19.0–20.0% due to its bimodal microstructure, which is formed by fine and coarse grain zones. These microstructural features lead to an isotropic behaviour of the mechanical properties. Varying the process parameters, yield strength and ultimate tensile strength can reach values higher than 300 MPa and 400 MPa, respectively, maintaining an isotropic behaviour. After direct aging heat treatment (325 °C × 4 h), the yield and ultimate tensile strength values increase up to 456–469 MPa and 512–521 MPa, respectively, while the strain decreases to 12.0–13.0% due to phase precipitation in the α-Al matrix. Notably, the bimodal microstructure remains largely unchanged. The HIP treatment, carried out at 325 °C × 4 h with a pressure of 1000 bar, reduced the porosity (approximatively 0.18%), resulting in further improvements. The yield strength and the ultimate tensile strength rose to 482–493 MPa and 523–547 MPa, respectively.

Abstract:
One of the most important factors during Laser Powder Bed Fusion is a robust and stable process to generate reproducibly dense and crack-free components with the same homogenous and fine-grained microstructure. Among other factors, surface tension influences the robustness of this process. Three aluminum alloys were investigated by means of 3D laser printing with respect to their ability to form lightweight and high-performance structures. The alloys include two Al-Cr based alloys (Zicromal®: Al-Cr-Zr-Mn, Scancromal®: Al-Cr-Sc-Zr) and an Al-Mg based alloy (Scalmalloy®: Al-Mg-Sc-Mn-Zr). The surface tensions of their liquid melts were measured by means of the oscillating droplet method in electromagnetic levitation. Scalmalloy® exhibited a surface tension that was by 3-8% smaller than the other two alloys, over a temperature range of 500 K above their liquidus temperature; the evaporation analysis showed that Scancromal® exhibits significantly less evaporation compared to the other two alloys by an order of magnitude. During the Laser Powder Bed Fusion process, Scalmalloy® presented the most unstable melt dynamics, and Scancromal® appeared to be more robust and stable with less weld spatters and negligible dust deposition, as evidence from the high-speed video observations. The results support the idea that surface tension and evaporation are potentially crucial factors influencing the melt dynamics and also demonstrate the capability of additive manufacturing that produces customized aluminum alloys for aerospace applications.

Abstract:
Fabrication of high strength aluminum alloys using laser-based powder bed fusion (L-PBF) encounters challenges, including the occurrence of solidification cracks and the loss of volatile elements, such as Zn and Mg. The current work developed a Si-modified Al7075 alloy aiming at introducing eutectic phases to mitigate the solidification cracking during L-PBF. Based on Kou’s model, the addition of Zn and Mg decreased the crack susceptibility from 6504 °C to 5966 °C, and the addition of 3.74 wt pct of Si further decreased the crack susceptibility to 3960 °C. The Al7075 alloy fabricated by L-PBF exhibited a large amount of solidification cracks extending throughout the sample. Crack-free samples with a relative density of 99.94 pct, as inspected by X-ray microcomputed tomography, were achieved for the developed Si-modified Al7075 alloy. The microstructure showed a transition from a coarse columnar microstructure to a refined mixed columnar + equiaxed microstructure after alloy modification, with a concomitant grain size reduction from 59.0 ± 42.2 to 15.0 ± 9.4 µ m. Moreover, Si, Mg 2 Si, and Al 2 Cu phases were detected in the Si-modified Al7075 alloy. After a direct ageing heat treatment, the Si-modified Al7075 alloy showed minimal age hardening effect with a peak hardness of (146 ± 3 Hv).

Abstract:
A critical issue in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) additive manufacturing is the selective vaporization of alloying elements resulting in poor mechanical properties and corrosion resistance of parts. The process also alters the part’s chemical composition compared to the feedstock. Here we present a novel multi-physics modeling framework, integrating heat and fluid flow simulations, thermodynamic calculations, and evaporation modeling to estimate and control the composition change during LPBF of nickel-based superalloys. Experimental validation confirms the accuracy of our model. Moreover, we quantify the relative vulnerabilities of different nickel-based superalloys to composition change quantitatively and we examine the effect of remelting due to the layer-by-layer deposition during the LPBF process. Spatial variations in evaporative flux and compositions for each element were determined, providing valuable insights into the LPBF process and product attributes. The results of this study can be used to optimize the LPBF process parameters such as laser power, scanning speed, and powder layer thickness to ensure the production of high-quality components with desired chemical compositions.

Abstract:
The study investigated the use of electron beam powder bed fusion (EB-PBF) to fabricate niobium ATI C103™ alloy articles for microstructural characterization and mechanical testing. The feedstock powder was consolidated into low-porosity articles, and both powder and sample chemistry were monitored. Oxygen uptake in the powder was limited to less than the ASTM B655/B655M (2018) specification limits for 7 uses. Manipulating vacuum chamber pressure showed stable hafnium content but decreasing titanium content with decreasing chamber pressure attributed to evaporation. AM samples were evaluated in the post-processed, as-fabricated, annealed, and hot isostatic pressing (HIP) condition with a maximum yield strength of 287 MPa, UTS of 375 MPa for the HIP, and maximum elongation of 32 pct for the annealed specimens, respectively. Mechanical properties are similar to typical wrought products, with a notable increase in yield strength after post-processing by HIP. The fracture behavior was driven by porosity in the as-fabricated specimens and grain boundary fracture after HIP.

Abstract:
<jats:p>A laser powder bed fusion process operating at elevated temperatures is introduced capable of fabricating crack-free and dense intermetallic titanium aluminide alloy specimens as well as demonstrator components using a base plate heating up to 900 °C and a unique heating system of the uppermost powder bed layer up to 1200 °C. Two so-called 4th generation alloys, TNM and TNM+, were used for this study. The microstructure and its evolution during subsequent heat treatments were investigated and explained by employing scanning electron microscopy, hardness testing, X-ray diffraction, differential scanning calorimetry and thermodynamic equilibrium calculation. Selected specimens were subjected to creep tests at 750 °C. The microstructures after processing consist of extraordinarily fine lamellar γ-TiAl/α2-Ti3Al-colonies with globular γ and βo-TiAl grains for both the TNM and TNM+ alloy, exhibiting a microstructure gradient from the last consolidated powder layer down to the starting layer due to cellular reaction, which increases the amount of globular γ and βo at the boundaries of the γ/α2-colonies. During annealing in proximity to the γ-solvus temperature, banded microstructures might form, as the α-grain size is only partially controlled by heterogeneously distributed γ/β-phase, which stems from the process-related Al loss. Additionally, the occurrence of thermally-induced porosity is investigated. Optimizing the microstructure to a homogenized, almost fully lamellar microstructure, involved annealing in the β-single phase field region and led to improved creep properties. Finally, TNM demonstrator components with complex geometries, such as aero engine blades and turbocharger turbine wheels, are fabricated by employing the novel laser powder bed fusion process.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:p>Metal additive manufacturing (AM) generates complex microstructures through extreme thermal gradients and rapid solidification, critically influencing mechanical performance and industrial qualification. This review synthesizes recent advances in cellular automata (CA) and phase-field (PF) modeling to predict grain-scale microstructure evolution during AM. CA methods provide computational efficiency, enabling large-domain simulations and excelling in texture prediction and multi-layer builds. PF approaches deliver superior thermodynamic fidelity for interface dynamics, solute partitioning, and nonequilibrium rapid solidification through CALPHAD coupling. Hybrid CA–PF frameworks strategically balance efficiency and accuracy by allocating PF to solidification fronts and CA to bulk grain competition. Recent algorithmic innovations—discrete event-inspired CA, GPU acceleration, and machine learning—extend scalability while maintaining predictive capability. Validated applications across Ni-based superalloys, Ti-6Al-4V, tool steels, and Al alloys demonstrate robust process–microstructure–property predictions through EBSD and mechanical testing. Persistent challenges include computational scalability for full-scale components, standardized calibration protocols, limited in situ validation, and incomplete multi-physics coupling. Emerging solutions leverage physics-informed machine learning, digital twin architectures, and open-source platforms to enable predictive microstructure control for first-time-right manufacturing in aerospace, biomedical, and energy applications.</jats:p>

Abstract:
Synchrotron and laboratory-based X-ray imaging techniques have been increasingly used for in situ investigations of alloy solidification and other metal processes. Several reviews have been published in recent years that have focused on the development of in situ X-ray imaging techniques for metal solidification studies. Instead, this work provides a comprehensive review of knowledge provided by in situ X-ray imaging for improved understanding of solidification theories and emerging metal processing technologies. We first review insights related to crystal nucleation and growth mechanisms gained by in situ X-ray imaging, including solute suppressed nucleation theory of α-Al and intermetallic compound crystals, dendritic growth of α-Al and the twin plane re-entrant growth mechanism of faceted Fe-rich intermetallics. Second, we discuss the contribution of in situ X-ray studies in understanding microstructural instability, including dendrite fragmentation induced by solute-driven, dendrite root re-melting, instability of a planar solid/liquid interface, the cellular-to-dendritic transition and the columnar-to-equiaxed transition. Third, we review investigations of defect formation mechanisms during near-equilibrium solidification, including porosity and hot tear formation, and the associated liquid metal flow. Then, we discuss how X-ray imaging is being applied to the understanding and development of emerging metal processes that operate further from equilibrium, such as additive manufacturing. Finally, the outlook for future research opportunities and challenges is presented.

Abstract:
In the last two decades, X-ray imaging techniques have been used increasingly to study metal solidification in real-time as, thanks to advances in X-ray sources (synchrotron and laboratory-based) and detector technology, images can now be obtained with spatio-temporal resolutions sufficient to record key phenomena and extract quantitative information, primarily relating to crystal growth. This paper presents an overview of the research conducted at the University of Oxford over the last 6 years as a partner in the UK’s Future Liquid Metal Engineering (LiME) Manufacturing Hub. The focus is on in situ X-ray radiography to investigate the solidification of Al alloys, including the formation of primary α-Al crystals, and the formation and growth of secondary intermetallic phases. Technologically, the thrust is to understand how to control as-cast phases, structures and element distributions, particularly elements associated with recycling, as a means to facilitate greater recirculation of aluminium alloys. We first present studies on refinement of primary α-Al, including extrinsic grain refinement using inoculation and intrinsic refinement based on dendrite fragmentation. Second, we describe studies on intermetallic phase formation and growth, because intermetallic fraction, morphology and distribution are frequently a limiting factor of alloy mechanical properties and recyclability. Then we present some of the latest progress in studying liquid flow during solidification and associated hot tear formation. Finally, future research directions are described.

Abstract:
Cooling Rate (CR) definitively influences the microstructure of metallic parts manufactured through various processes. Factors including cooling medium, surface area, thermal conductivity, and temperature control can influence both predicted and unforeseen impacts that then influence the results of mechanical properties. This comprehensive study explores the impact of CRs in diffusion, microstructural development, and the characterization of aluminum alloys and the influence of various manufacturing processes and post-process treatments, and it studies analytical models that can predict their effects. It examines a broad range of CRs encountered in diverse manufacturing methods, such as laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), directed energy deposition (DED), casting, forging, welding, and hot isostatic pressing (HIP). For example, varying CRs might result in different types of solidification and microstructural evolution in aluminum alloys, which thereby influence their mechanical properties during end use. The study further examines the effects of post-process heat treatments, including quenching, annealing, and precipitation hardening, on the microstructure and mechanical properties of aluminum alloys. It discusses numerical and analytical models, which are used to predict and optimize CRs for achieving targeted material characteristics of specific aluminum alloys. Although understanding CR and its effects is crucial, there is a lack of literature on how CR affects alloy properties. This comprehensive review aims to bridge the knowledge gap through a thorough literature review of the impact of CR on microstructure and mechanical properties.

Abstract:
Magnesium-based alloy WE43 is a state-of-the-art bioresorbable metallic implant material. There is a need for implants with both complex geometries to match the mechanical properties of bone and refined microstructure for controlled resorption. Additive manufacturing (AM) using laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) presents a viable fabrication method for implant applications, as it offers near-net-shape geometrical control, allows for geometry customization based on an individual patient, and fast cooling rates to achieve a refined microstructure. In this study, the laser–alloy interaction is investigated over a range of LPBF-relevant processing conditions to reveal melt-pool dynamics, pore formation, and the microstructure of laser-melted WE43. In situ X-ray imaging reveals distinct laser-induced vapor depression morphology regimes, with minimal pore formation at laser-scan speeds greater than 500 mm/s. Optical and electron microscopy of cross-sectioned laser tracks reveal three distinct microstructural regimes that can be controlled by adjusting laser-scan parameters: columnar, dendritic, and banded microstructures. These regimes are consistent with those predicted by the analytic solidification theory for conduction-mode welding, but not for keyhole-mode tracks. The results provide insight into the fundamental laser–material interactions of the WE43 alloy under AM-processing conditions and are critical for the successful implementation of LPBF-produced WE43 parts in biomedical applications.
