Abstract:
Spatter during laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) can induce surface defects, impacting the fatigue performance of the fabricated components. Here, we reveal and explain the links between vapour depression shape and spatter dynamics during LPBF of an Al-Fe-Zr aluminium alloy using high-speed synchrotron x-ray imaging. We quantify the number, trajectory angle, velocity, and kinetic energy of the spatter as a function of vapour depression zone/keyhole morphology under industry-relevant processing conditions. The depression zone/keyhole morphology was found to influence the spatter ejection angle in keyhole versus conduction melting modes: (i) the vapour-pressure driven plume in conduction mode with a quasi-semi-circular depression zone leads to backward spatter whereas; and (ii) the keyhole rear wall redirects the gas/vapour flow to cause vertical spatter ejection and rear rim droplet spatter. Increasing the opening of the keyhole or vapour depression zone can reduce entrainment of solid spatter. We discover a spatter-induced cavity mechanism in which small spatter particles are accelerated towards the powder bed after laser-spatter interaction, inducing powder denudation and cavities on the printed surface. By quantifying these laser-spatter interactions, we suggest a printing strategy for minimising defects and improving the surface quality of LPBF parts.

Abstract:
Spatter is an inherent, unpreventable, and undesired phenomenon in laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) additive manufacturing. Spatter behavior has an intrinsic correlation with the forming quality in L-PBF because it leads to metallurgical defects and the degradation of mechanical properties. This impact becomes more severe in the fabrication of large-sized parts during the multi-laser L-PBF process. Therefore, investigations of spatter generation and countermeasures have become more urgent. Although much research has provided insights into the melt pool, microstructure, and mechanical property, reviews of spatter in L-PBF are still limited. This work reviews the literature on the in situ detection, generation, effects, and countermeasures of spatter in L-PBF. It is expected to pave the way towards a novel generation of highly efficient and intelligent L-PBF systems.

Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) is of great importance for the visual measurement and analysis of the metallization process, which is the process of solid, liquid, and gas phase transformations of metal powders under high-energy laser irradiation due to the low boiling point/high saturated vapor pressure. Since the evaporation of metals involves the interaction of driving forces such as vapor back pressure, surface tension, and gravity, the movement of the melt pool is not stable. At the same time, it also produces vaporization products such as vapor plumes and sprays, which cause defects such as bubbles, porosity, lack of fusion, inclusions, etc., during the manufacturing process of the parts, affecting the performance and manufacturing quality of the parts. More and more researchers are using imaging technologies, such as high-speed X-ray, high-speed visible light cameras, and high-speed schlieren imaging, to perform noncontact visual measurements and analyses of the melt pool, vapor plume, and spatter during the metal evaporation process, and the results show that the metal evaporation process can be suppressed by optimizing the process parameters and changing the processing atmosphere, thereby reducing part defects and improving part performance and built part quality. This paper reviews the research on metal evaporation mechanisms and visual measurement methods of metal evaporation, then discusses the measures of metal evaporation, and finally summarizes and prospects the future research hotspots of LPBF technology, according to the existing scholars’ research on numerical simulation analysis and visual measurement methods of the metal evaporation process.

Abstract:
Although metal vaporisation has been observed in several laser processes such as drilling or welding, vapour plume expansion and its induced side effects are not fully understood. Especially, this phenomenon is garnering scientific and industrial interest since recent investigations in laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) have designated metal vaporisation as main source of denudation and powder spattering. The present study aims to provide a new insight on the dynamics of laser-induced vaporisation and to assess the potential of different gases for particle entrainment. A self-consistent finite element model of laser-induced keyhole and plume is thus presented for this purpose, built from a comprehensive literature review. The model is validated with dedicated experimental diagnostics, involving high-speed imaging to measure the ascent velocity of the vapour plume. The transient dynamics of vapour plume is thus quantified for different laser incident intensities and gas flow patterns such as the mushroom-like structure of the vapour plume are analysed. Finally, the model is used as a tool to quantify the entrainment flow expected in LPBF and an analytical model is derived to define a velocity threshold for particle entrainment, expressed in term of background gas properties. Doing so it is possible to predict how denudation evolves when the gaseous atmosphere is changed.

Abstract:
Powder spattering and splashing in the melt pool are common phenomena during Laser-based Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) of metallic materials having high fluidity. For this purpose, analytical and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) models have been deduced for the LPBF of AlSi10Mg alloy. The single printed layer’s dimensions were estimated using primary operating conditions for the analytical model. In CFD modelling, the volume of fluid and discrete element modelling techniques were applied to illustrate the splashing and spatter phenomena, providing a novel hydrodynamics CFD model for LPBF of AlSi10Mg alloy. The computational results were compared with the experimental analyses. A trial-and-error method was used to propose an optimized set of parameters for the LPBF of AlSi10Mg alloy. Laser scanning speed, laser spot diameter and laser power were changed. On the other hand, the powder layer thickness and hatch distance were kept constant. Following on, 20 samples were fabricated using the LPBF process. The printed samples’ microstructures were used to select optimized parameters for achieving defect-free parts. It was found that the recoil pressure, vaporization, high-speed vapor cloud, Marangoni flow, hydraulic pressure and buoyancy are all controlled by the laser-material interaction time. As the laser-AlSi10Mg material interaction period progresses, the forces presented above become dominant. Splashing occurs due to a combination of increased recoil pressure, laser-material interaction time, higher material’s fluidity, vaporization, dominancy of Marangoni flow, high-speed vapor cloud, hydraulic pressure, buoyancy, and transformation of keyhole from J-shape to reverse triangle-shape that is a tongue-like protrusion in the keyhole. In the LPBF of AlSi10Mg alloy, only the conduction mode melt flow has been determined. For multi-layers printing of AlSi10Mg alloy, the optimum operating conditions are laser power = 140 W, laser spot diameter = 180 µm, laser scanning speed = 0.6 m/s, powder layer thickness = 50 µm and hatch distance = 112 µm. These conditions have been identified using sample microstructures.

Abstract:

Purpose
There is recent emphasis on designing new materials and alloys specifically for metal additive manufacturing (AM) processes, in contrast to AM of existing alloys that were developed for other traditional manufacturing methods involving considerably different physics. Process optimization to determine processing recipes for newly developed materials is expensive and time-consuming. The purpose of the current work is to use a systematic printability assessment framework developed by the co-authors to determine windows of processing parameters to print defect-free parts from a binary nickel-niobium alloy (NiNb5) using laser powder bed fusion (LPBF) metal AM.


Design/methodology/approach
The printability assessment framework integrates analytical thermal modeling, uncertainty quantification and experimental characterization to determine processing windows for NiNb5 in an accelerated fashion. Test coupons and mechanical test samples were fabricated on a ProX 200 commercial LPBF system. A series of density, microstructure and mechanical property characterization was conducted to validate the proposed framework.


Findings
Near fully-dense parts with more than 99% density were successfully printed using the proposed framework. Furthermore, the mechanical properties of as-printed parts showed low variability, good tensile strength of up to 662 MPa and tensile ductility 51% higher than what has been reported in the literature.


Originality/value
Although many literature studies investigate process optimization for metal AM, there is a lack of a systematic printability assessment framework to determine manufacturing process parameters for newly designed AM materials in an accelerated fashion. Moreover, the majority of existing process optimization approaches involve either time- and cost-intensive experimental campaigns or require the use of proprietary computational materials codes. Through the use of a readily accessible analytical thermal model coupled with statistical calibration and uncertainty quantification techniques, the proposed framework achieves both efficiency and accessibility to the user. Furthermore, this study demonstrates that following this framework results in printed parts with low degrees of variability in their mechanical properties.

The integrating-sphere method measures scattered light from the weld using two calibrated InGaAs photodiodes: one detects light scattered back toward the weld head, while the other collects diffusely scattered light through the sphere. The absorbed power is calculated as input power minus the weld-head and integrating-sphere signals, Pabs(t) = P0(t) − [Phead(t) + Psphere(t)], and dynamic absorptance is A(t) = Pabs(t)/P0(t). Integrating-sphere calibration uses a diffuse gold target and includes an attenuation-filter transmission correction. Calorimetry independently estimates total absorbed energy from the sample mass, specific heat, and corrected initial temperature rise, E0 = mCpΔT0. Thermal losses are corrected by fitting the post-pulse thermocouple decay. Abstract:
Laser powder bed fusion (L-PBF) has attracted significant attention in both the industry and academic fields since its inception, providing unprecedented advantages to fabricate complex-shaped metallic components. The printing quality and performance of L-PBF alloys are influenced by numerous variables consisting of feedstock powders, manufacturing process, and post-treatment. As the starting materials, metallic powders play a critical role in influencing the fabrication cost, printing consistency, and properties. Given their deterministic roles, the present review aims to retrospect the recent progress on metallic powders for L-PBF including characterization, preparation, and reuse. The powder characterization mainly serves for printing consistency while powder preparation and reuse are introduced to reduce the fabrication costs. Various powder characterization and preparation methods are presented in the beginning by analyzing the measurement principles, advantages, and limitations. Subsequently, the effect of powder reuse on the powder characteristics and mechanical performance of L-PBF parts is analyzed, focusing on steels, nickel-based superalloys, titanium and titanium alloys, and aluminum alloys. The evolution trends of powders and L-PBF parts vary depending on specific alloy systems, which makes the proposal of a unified reuse protocol infeasible. Finally, perspectives are presented to cater to the increased applications of L-PBF technologies for future investigations. The present state-of-the-art work can pave the way for the broad industrial applications of L-PBF by enhancing printing consistency and reducing the total costs from the perspective of powders.

Metal powders are key to metal additive manufacturing technologies such as powder bed fusion. To evaluate such effects, these powders need to be characterized, tested, and analyzed at critical stages of their lifecycles. This paper provides a review of the current state of the art for powder evaluation methods and their applicability for powder bed fusion production. Abstract:
The flowability of a powder is a characteristic dependent on both the particle ensemble's physical properties as well as the testing equipment and conditions. In powder bed additive manufacturing processes (SLM, EBM), flowability can be used to predict the quality of the deposited powder layer. However, how representative flowability is for the powder bed layer quality is not always clear. In this work, we compared several steel powders, as well as different testing methods. Each powder had an individual combination of composition or particle size distribution. Furthermore, the flowability testing equipment and methods were selected according to standards (Tap density, Hall flow) or referring to the published literature (angle of repose, FT4 Powder Rheometer). After measuring the flowability of different samples for each testing method, we created a database to evaluate a first correlation between the different testing methods. Finally, with a Powder Rheometer, we investigated for one sample some flow properties as function of different particle size distributions.

Abstract:
<jats:p>Melt-pool depth governs interlayer bonding and porosity in laser powder bed fusion and underpins part qualification, yet predicting it reliably remains difficult. Fast conduction models reach useful accuracy only after the absorptivity is fitted to the depths they are meant to predict, and inverse analyses have been used the same way, to recover a calibrated parameter rather than to test the model. Here, the absorptivity is fixed independently instead, a measured coupling for IN718 and, for IN625 and 316L, a published closed-form relation never fitted to the present depths. This converts a moving-source conduction model from an object of calibration into one of validation. The melt boundary is located by root-finding rather than on a grid, so no discretization error enters the diagnosis. Across 231 single tracks, the model reproduces conduction-regime depth and half-width to within a few percent and underpredicts increasingly once keyholing begins. Inverting each measured depth for the absorptivity conduction would require yielding a fitting-free diagnosis: no conduction-regime track demands a non-physical value, and the inferred value converges near 0.38 against inputs of 0.27 to 0.34, whereas every keyhole-classified track demands a value above unity. Because an inferred absorptivity also absorbs unmodeled transport, downward convection was emulated as an anisotropic effective diffusivity; at the enhancement reported for Marangoni flow, no keyhole track becomes explicable. A measured Ti-6Al-4V absorptivity rise of a factor 1.9 supports the mechanism. An enthalpy-indexed correction and data-driven baselines remain alloy-specific, whereas the physics-based model retains its advantage under cross-alloy extrapolation. All findings are for single tracks on bare plates.</jats:p>

Abstract:
<jats:title>Abstract</jats:title>
                  <jats:p>Significant advances have been made in the field of Additive Manufacturing (AM) across various manufacturing processes. Laser Powder Bed Fusion (LPBF) is one of the most widely adopted metal AM processes in the industry, which employs energy sources such as lasers to melt powder materials. While the LPBF process offers numerous advantages, such as the ability to produce complex geometries and multiple parts simultaneously, it also presents challenges in the form of defects such as porosity, residual stresses, and cracks that need to be addressed. Conducting experiments to identify and eliminate these defects can be prohibitively expensive, motivating the development of alternative predictive approaches. Numerical modeling and simulation techniques provide a cost-effective alternative to experimental approaches, enabling analyses ranging from thermal histories and microstructural evolution to mechanical property prediction and defect identification in fabricated components. However, such simulations can also be computationally intensive. In recent years, Machine Learning (ML) and Artificial Intelligence (AI) algorithms have emerged as viable alternative tools to accelerate process understanding, defect prediction, and parameter optimization. This review provides a comprehensive overview of ML-based approaches applied to LPBF, emphasizing the importance of understanding the underlying physical phenomena that significantly influence data collection, preprocessing, and feature engineering strategies essential for effective model training and validation. It offers a structured framework for researchers seeking to leverage ML methods to enhance predictive accuracy and computational efficiency, particularly through simulation-driven data generation for model development.</jats:p>

The excerpt describes a simplified analytical Gaussian moving-heat-source model for predicting melt-pool temperature fields and dimensions. It states that analytical or semi-analytical thermal models can estimate melt-pool width, length, and depth, and that the study adapts a model from Schuöcker (1998). The temperature field is expressed as a function of baseplate temperature, absorptivity, laser power, thermal conductivity, beam radius, scanning speed, thermal diffusivity, density, and heat capacity. The model uses the Hagen–Rubens relation to estimate absorptivity from electrical resistivity and laser wavelength. For powder beds, density, absorptivity/emissivity, and thermal conductivity are corrected using porosity and powder-bed formulations. Material properties are treated as constant and evaluated at 80% of the melting temperature because prior work found this produced the smallest discrepancies between calculated and measured melt-pool sizes. The excerpt explains that model predictions are assessed using in-situ dual-wavelength thermal imaging and ex-situ single-track metallography, providing width, length, depth, and surface-temperature data. The excerpt describes complementary approaches for characterizing LPBF spatter and vapor-plume behavior in aluminum alloys. High-speed optical and Schlieren imaging have been used to observe spatter and the vapor plume above the powder surface, but these methods do not provide detailed information about changes in vapor-depression or keyhole morphology. High-speed synchrotron x-ray imaging addresses this limitation by capturing both melt-pool/keyhole dynamics and spatter, with temporal resolution reported as high as 1 MHz. The study quantifies spatter number, trajectory angle, velocity, and kinetic energy, and relates ejection angle to depression-zone/keyhole morphology. The abstract identifies distinct behavior associated with melting mode: conduction-mode vapor pressure produces backward spatter, while the keyhole rear wall redirects gas/vapor flow and produces more vertical ejection and rear-rim droplet spatter. The excerpt does not specify camera models, illumination systems, or conventional optical frame rates, nor does it provide a direct aluminum-versus-steel comparison. It does establish the quality relevance: oversized spatter can increase surface defects and roughness, become trapped in later layers and cause lack-of-fusion porosity, oxidize powder, inhibit fusion, and reduce part density. Small spatter can also induce powder denudation and surface cavities after laser-spatter interaction.

For each category, include: Measurement, Method(s)/Equipment, Key Standards, Sample Requirements, Key Equations/Criteria, Typical Uncertainties, and key Published Example DOIs. Categories: 1) Melt pool geometry, 2) Laser absorptivity, 3) Thermal history/cooling rate, 4) CET/grain structure, 5) Composition change, 6) Printability maps, 7) Residual stress, 8) Spatter/plume, 9) Powder properties."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-00)

| # | Measurement | Method(s) / typical equipment | Key standards | Sample requirements | Key equations / criteria | Typical uncertainty / limitation | Published examples |
|---:|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Melt-pool width, depth, length and melting mode | Optical/SEM top views; transverse and longitudinal metallographic sections; calibrated microscope and ImageJ/Fiji; optional coaxial or off-axis high-speed imaging. Mount, grind and polish; etch Al with Keller’s or Weck’s reagent and Cu alloys with FeCl₃–HCl, ammonium persulfate or Klemm-type reagent after alloy-specific trials. Measure at least 3 transverse sections per track—preferably 5–8—and one longitudinal section; omit acceleration/deceleration zones. | ASTM E3 and E407; ASTM E112 where grain size is also measured | Approximately 20–40 parameter combinations; 2 replicate tracks per condition; tracks ≥5–10 mm. Use a bare plate and a nominal powder layer where possible because coupling differs. | Aspect ratio: `AR = d/w`; conduction generally `d/w < 0.5`, transition near 0.5, keyhole generally `d/w > 0.5`. King criterion is equivalently `d/(w/2) > 1`; reported normalized-enthalpy transition `ΔH/h_s ≈ 30 ± 4`. LOF risk if `d < t`; overlap criterion `(h/w)² + (t/d)² ≤ 1`. Fit absorptivity and, only if independently uncertain, beam radius by minimizing weighted width/depth/length residuals; validate on held-out tracks. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000033) | Well-polished cross-sections commonly give ±2–5 µm edge-location error and 5–10% repeatability; along-track instability can dominate, especially in transition/keyhole mode. A single section is inadequate. | King et al., **10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2014.06.005**; Caprio et al., **10.3390/met12101762**; Tenbrock et al., **10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2019.116514**; Bergmueller et al., **10.1007/s00170-023-11377-2** |
| 2 | Effective laser absorptivity at approximately 1070 nm | **Calorimetry:** thermally isolated metal disk or coupon, embedded thermocouples, known heat capacity and laser trajectory; compare temperature rise with incident energy. **Integrating sphere:** gold-coated sphere, calibrated InGaAs detectors for sphere and back-reflected channels, reference diffuse-gold target; sub-microsecond acquisition is possible. Test polished bulk, as-received surface and controlled powder layers separately. | Detector calibration traceable to radiometric standards; no single LPBF-specific absorptivity standard | At least 3 repeats for each surface state and several power–speed conditions spanning no melt, conduction, transition and keyhole. Trapp used approximately 100 µm powder layers. | `A_eff = E_abs/E_L`; calorimetry: `E_abs = m∫C_p(T)dT`, `E_L = P L/v`; sphere: `A(t) = 1 − [P_sphere(t)+P_head(t)]/P_0(t)` when transmission is negligible. Clean bulk Cu is about 0.03–0.05 and loose Cu powder about 0.12–0.20 at low intensity; measured Cu powder rose toward approximately 0.53 near keyholing. Powder and keyhole values must not be replaced by room-temperature Fresnel data. (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000006, pqac-00000007, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010) | Calorimetry typically about ±5–10% relative after heat-loss correction; integrating-sphere radiometry can reach a few percent after port, filter and detector calibration. Calorimetry may underestimate coupling if vaporized/ejected mass carries unmeasured enthalpy. | Trapp et al., **10.1016/j.apmt.2017.08.006**; Simonds et al., **10.1103/PhysRevApplied.10.044061**; Gargalis et al., **10.1016/j.jmatprotec.2021.117130**; Ye et al., **10.1002/adem.201900185** |
| 3 | Thermal history, peak temperature, thermal gradient `G`, solidification rate `R` and cooling rate | Fine K- or N-type thermocouples embedded in substrate near tracks; two-colour pyrometer; calibrated MWIR/SWIR high-speed camera with spectral filters; post-mortem SEM measurement of cellular or dendrite-arm spacing; high-speed synchrotron radiography/diffraction for melt boundary, keyhole and solidification front. | ITS-90 traceability for temperature calibration; ASTM E230/E230M for thermocouples | ≥3 instrumented repeats per representative condition; use several known camera/pyrometer calibration temperatures. For spacing proxies, measure ≥100 intercepts or cells across pool boundary, centre and trailing region on ≥3 tracks. | `R = v cosθ`, where `θ` is between scan direction and local interface normal/growth direction; `Ṫ = G R`; spacing proxy `λ = A(Ṫ)^{-n}`. Determine `A,n` for the specific alloy/microstructural metric rather than importing a casting correlation. LPBF Al commonly lies around `10⁵–10⁷ K s⁻¹`. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020) | Embedded thermocouples are bandwidth- and distance-limited and may under-read melt temperature by hundreds of kelvin. Two-colour pyrometry commonly ±2–5% if grey-body assumptions hold; single-colour IR can be wrong by >10% without dynamic emissivity. Spacing-derived cooling rate is often uncertain by a factor of approximately 2–3. | Guo et al., **10.1016/j.addma.2019.04.021**; Huang et al., **10.1038/s41467-022-28694-x**; Soderlind et al., **10.3390/cryst12101437**; Rahman et al., **10.3390/machines13020160** |
| 4 | Columnar-to-equiaxed transition, grain size and crystallographic texture | EBSD on longitudinal build/scan sections and pad top surfaces; field-emission SEM with EBSD detector; optional EDS/TEM for Al₃(Sc,Zr). Final polish with colloidal silica or low-energy ion milling. Map entire melt pools at coarse step and boundary/centre regions at ≤0.05–0.2 µm for submicrometre Sc/Zr-refined grains. | ASTM E2627 for EBSD orientation analysis; ASTM E112 for conventional grain size | ≥3 melt pools or tracks per condition; ≥3 EBSD fields in pool boundary, centre and remelted zones; target ≥500–1000 indexed grains for robust size and texture statistics. | Report equivalent-circle diameter, aspect ratio, equiaxed area fraction, grain-boundary misorientation and texture index/MUD. Compare local modeled `(G,R)` with Hunt/KGT-type CET maps: `GR` controls cooling rate while `G/R` strongly influences morphology. Sc/Zr systems require nucleant density and undercooling terms; thermal criteria alone are not sufficient. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025) | Grain-size uncertainty is commonly 5–15% when several fields are pooled; equiaxed fraction approximately ±3–5 percentage points. Step sizes too large for the fine boundary zone systematically overestimate grain size and create false texture. | Lu et al., **10.3390/cryst13060913**; Michi et al., **10.1080/09506608.2021.1951580**; Cerri et al., **10.3390/cryst15010025** |
| 5 | Selective evaporation and composition drift—especially Mg, Zn, Li and brass Zn | Bulk powder and printed-pad/coupon chemistry by ICP-OES or ICP-MS after complete dissolution; EPMA/WDS for spatial maps; EDS only for screening; collect condensate/spatter where possible. Use multiple printed conditions spanning absorbed line energy and melting mode. | ASTM E3061 for ICP-AES analysis of Al alloys; laboratory digestion and certified-reference-material procedures | Preserve ≥5–10 g virgin powder for chemistry; print ≥3 pads/coupons at low, nominal and high energy. Digest ≥3 independent aliquots from powder and from each printed condition; sample the coupon interior rather than only oxidized surfaces. | Element loss: `L_i = (C_{i,powder}−C_{i,print})/C_{i,powder} ×100%`. Relate to absorbed line energy `A P/v`, not only nominal volumetric energy. Langmuir/Hertz–Knudsen flux: `J_i = α_i a_i p_i^{sat}(T)√[M_i/(2πRT)]`, integrated over melt surface area and lifetime; include gas shielding and activity. (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027) | ICP-OES commonly 1–3% relative for major elements and 3–10% near detection limits; sampling heterogeneity can dominate. SEM-EDS is generally unsuitable for detecting approximately 1% relative Mg loss. | Bärtl et al., **10.1007/s11665-022-06592-z**; Li et al., **10.1007/s11661-020-06073-9**; Mukherjee et al., **10.1038/s41524-024-01418-z** |
| 6 | Printability maps: LOF, balling, keyhole porosity, density and hot cracking | Stage 1: top-view microscopy/profilometry of single tracks. Stage 2: single-layer pads at several hatch spacings. Stage 3: small 5–10 mm cubes. Density by polished-section image analysis, Archimedes and preferably micro-CT for defect morphology. Crack density by stitched optical/SEM images and skeletonized line-length analysis. | ASTM B962 for Archimedes density; ASTM E3 for metallography; ASTM E1245 for automated image analysis; ASTM E1441 for CT guidance | Efficient design: 20–30 power–speed tracks, two replicates; 8–12 pads covering candidate window/hatch spacings; 6–12 confirmation cubes. Use randomized positions and include centre/edge locations. | LOF: `d<t` or failed overlap `(h/w)²+(t/d)²>1`; keyhole warning `d/w>0.5` plus rounded subsurface pores; balling commonly `L/w ≳2` and discontinuous track morphology. Relative density from images `ρ_rel = 1−A_pore/A_total`; crack density `CD = ΣL_crack/A`. Do not use `P/(vht)` as the sole map coordinate. (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000032, pqac-00000034) | Optical area fraction: approximately ±0.05–0.2 percentage points for dense material if ≥3 large fields/planes are used; Archimedes often ±0.1–0.5% and can exceed 100% because of wetting, trapped gas or uncertain theoretical density. CT detection is voxel-size limited. Crack density commonly varies 10–30% between fields. | Sheikh et al., **10.1038/s41524-024-01436-x**; Zhang et al., **10.1108/RPJ-01-2021-0024**; Yang et al., **10.1016/j.addma.2021.102103** |
| 7 | Residual stress and stress-relief distortion | Laboratory XRD `sin²ψ` for near-surface stress; bridge/alligator or cantilever release measured by optical profilometry/DIC; incremental hole drilling with strain gauge or ESPI; contour method for larger cross-sections; neutron diffraction for through-thickness lattice strain. | EN 15305 for XRD residual stress; ASTM E837 for hole drilling; ISO 21432 for neutron diffraction | XRD: ≥3 nominally identical coupons and several positions/directions. Bridge/cantilever: ≥3 repeats per condition and pre/post-release geometry. Contour and neutron methods usually require coupons thicker/larger than desktop calibration specimens. | `ε_φψ = (d_φψ−d₀)/d₀`; for biaxial stress, stress follows the slope of `d` or `2θ` versus `sin²ψ` using appropriate X-ray elastic constants. Cantilever/bridge distortion is compared directly with thermo-mechanical FE predictions; simple beam-curvature conversion is valid only when geometry and eigenstrain assumptions are satisfied. (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000039, pqac-00000041) | XRD is often ±20–50 MPa under favourable conditions but texture, coarse grains and uncertain stress-free `d₀` can dominate in Al/Cu. Hole drilling is commonly ±5–15%; release geometries show approximately 5–10% repeatability. Neutron uncertainty is often tens of MPa and spatial resolution is millimetric. | Representative LPBF methods summarized by Bertoli et al.; XRD/hole-drilling implementation evidence in (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036); released-cantilever/DIC example in (pqac-00000041) |
| 8 | Spatter, plume, denudation and melt-pool instability | Side-view high-speed visible imaging with narrow-band laser/LED illumination; coaxial imaging where available; schlieren with collimated source, knife edge and high-speed camera for gas-density gradients; particle tracking for count, size, velocity, angle and landing position; synchrotron X-ray imaging for subsurface correlation. | No mature LPBF-specific standard; document frame rate, exposure, magnification, thresholding and gas-flow conditions | Image ≥3 tracks per representative regime; 5–20 kfps is a practical minimum for plume/spatter, 50–100 kfps for droplet dynamics. Keep field of view several millimetres above and behind the pool; record no-laser background and spatial calibration. | Particle velocity `u = Δs/Δt`; kinetic energy `E_k = ½m u²` using equivalent-sphere mass; report event rate per track length/time, ejection-angle distribution and denuded width. In Al, Mg/Zn evaporation, oxide films and low density increase sensitivity to plume-driven entrainment and oxidized redeposition. (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000054, pqac-00000055) | Position is typically ±1–2 pixels; velocity about ±5–15% when particles persist for several frames. Particle mass/kinetic energy may be uncertain by >30% because diameter and temperature are poorly known. Schlieren is primarily qualitative unless carefully calibrated. | Guo et al., **10.1088/2631-7990/ad4e1d**; Li et al., **10.3390/mi13081366**; Liu et al., **10.3390/mi14071351**; Rehman et al., **10.3390/met11122023** |
| 9 | Powder PSD, morphology, flowability, packing density, O/H and moisture | Laser diffraction for volume PSD; dynamic image analysis/SEM for number PSD, satellites and shape; Hall/Carney funnel; rotating-drum avalanche or GranuDrum/Revolution analyzer; FT4 dynamic, aeration, permeability and shear tests; apparent/tap density; He pycnometry; LECO-type inert-gas-fusion O/N/H analyzer; Karl Fischer or controlled loss-on-drying/TGA for moisture. | ISO 13320; ISO 13322; ISO/ASTM 52907; ASTM B213 Hall; ASTM B964 Carney; ASTM B212 apparent density; ASTM B527 tap density; ASTM E1019 for O/N/H in applicable alloys; ASTM E1447 for H in Ti-based materials—not a universal Al/Cu method | Use representative riffled samples. Laser diffraction typically needs <1 g per repeat; imaging ≥10,000 particles; funnel tests commonly 50 g and may be unsuitable for cohesive Al powder; FT4 often 10–25 mL; chemistry approximately 0.1–1 g per replicate. Perform ≥3 repeats and retain an unopened baseline sample. | Report `D10/D50/D90`, span `(D90−D10)/D50`, circularity/sphericity, apparent and tap density. Hausner ratio `HR=ρ_tap/ρ_bulk`; Carr index `CI=100(ρ_tap−ρ_bulk)/ρ_tap`. Flow time alone does not predict spreadability; combine PSD/morphology, dynamic flow and a recoated-layer image or mass-per-area test. (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000044, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049) | Laser-diffraction repeatability is commonly 1–3% but assumes an optical model and near-spherical particles; image-analysis bias depends on segmentation and sampling. Funnel flow often has 2–5% repeatability or gives “no flow.” Inert-gas fusion commonly ±5–10% relative near low O/H concentrations; moisture is highly handling-dependent. | Gibbons et al., **10.1007/s40964-023-00484-x**; Brika et al., **10.1016/j.addma.2019.100929**; Sun et al., **10.1088/2631-7990/acfbc3** |


*Table: A practical comparison of nine calibration and validation measurement categories for LPBF aluminium and copper alloys, including equipment, sampling, equations, uncertainties, standards and peer-reviewed examples.*

function.arguments: {"artifact_type": "table", "description": "Create a ranked priority list table of the minimum set of measurements for calibrating an AM thermal model (Thermo-Calc AM Module or open alternatives like Eagar-Tsai) for a new Al alloy with only 100-300g of powder. Include columns for: Priority rank, Measurement, What it calibrates in the model, Minimum specimen count and powder consumption, and Notes. The top priorities should be: 1) Powder PSD/flowability/chemistry, 2) Single-track melt pool cross-sections, 3) Single-layer pad density/overlap, 4) Small cube density, 5) Microstructure (cell spacing for cooling rate), 6) Composition check (ICP-OES for evaporation), 7) EBSD for CET, 8) Residual stress (XRD), 9) Spatter/plume (optional). Include estimated powder usage for each."}
function.name: create_artifact

messages.content:
### Artifact (ID artifact-01)

| Priority rank | Measurement | What it calibrates or validates | Minimum specimen count and estimated powder use | Notes |
|---:|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Powder PSD, morphology, flow, packing, and chemistry | Powder-bed packing fraction, density, effective conductivity, initial alloy composition, and spreading reproducibility | Three riffled aliquots; 1–3 g for laser diffraction, 2–5 g for imaging, 30–50 g reusable for funnel testing or 10–25 mL reusable for rheometry, and 1–3 g for O/H and chemistry. Net irreversible use: about 5–10 g. | Record D10, D50, D90, morphology, apparent and tap density, O/H, moisture, and ICP-OES chemistry. For cohesive Al powder, supplement funnel tests with dynamic flow and recoated-layer mass per area. Retain an unopened baseline aliquot. (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000045, pqac-00000047, pqac-00000048, pqac-00000049) |
| 2 | Single-track top views and transverse and longitudinal melt-pool sections | Effective absorptivity and beam-radius calibration; width, depth, and length validation; conduction-to-keyhole boundary | Twenty to thirty power–speed conditions, two tracks per condition, at least three transverse sections per track, five near transition or keyhole, and selected longitudinal sections. About 5–15 g circulated; less than 1 g fused. | Include bare-plate and powder-layer tracks if possible. Measure the beam independently, fit absorptivity primarily to depth and width, and reserve 20–30% of conditions for validation. A depth-to-width ratio above about 0.5 warns of keyholing. (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000001, pqac-00000004, pqac-00000012, pqac-00000015) |
| 3 | Single-layer pad topography, continuity, overlap, and area porosity | Hatch-spacing and remelting calibration; transfer from isolated tracks to interacting tracks; LOF and balling boundaries | Eight to twelve pads of about 5 × 5 or 10 × 10 mm, using two or three hatch spacings. About 10–25 g circulated and 2–5 g fused. | Measure uncovered area, continuity, roughness, and overlap by optical mosaics or profilometry. Test the geometric overlap criterion but confirm it experimentally because conduction models omit melt flow, oxide films, and packing variability. (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031, pqac-00000033) |
| 4 | Small-cube or short-coupon density and pore morphology | Multilayer heat-accumulation and printability validation; separation of LOF from keyhole porosity | Six to twelve coupons, preferably 5 × 5 × 5 mm, including three repeats at the nominal condition and several boundary conditions. About 10–35 g fused and 30–80 g circulated. | Analyze at least three polished planes per condition. Use Archimedes as a secondary check; use micro-CT on two or three coupons to distinguish irregular LOF pores from rounded keyhole pores. (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000030, pqac-00000034) |
| 5 | Cellular or dendritic spacing across melt pools | Modeled cooling rate and spatial thermal-history validation after melt-pool calibration | Reuse sections from at least three low-, nominal-, and high-energy tracks or coupons; measure at least 100 cells or intercepts in pool-boundary, center, and trailing regions. No additional powder. | Establish or validate an alloy-specific spacing–cooling-rate relation. Do not import constants uncritically from cast Al-Si or another alloy. Estimate local solidification rate from scan speed and the measured interface orientation. (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018, pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020) |
| 6 | ICP-OES of virgin powder and low-, nominal-, and high-energy printed material | Selective-evaporation validation and the actual chemistry used for CALPHAD and thermophysical calculations | Three independent powder aliquots and three printed conditions, preferably with triplicate digestions. About 2–5 g of powder and 3–10 g of printed material consumed. | Sample coupon interiors. Report relative Mg, Zn, or Li loss and relate it to absorbed line energy and melt mode rather than nominal volumetric energy alone. Use EPMA/WDS for spatial segregation; EDS is generally inadequate for small bulk losses. (pqac-00000026, pqac-00000027) |
| 7 | EBSD grain size, texture, and columnar-to-equiaxed transition | Validation of derived thermal-gradient and solidification-rate fields and Hunt/KGT-type CET predictions | Reuse one nominal pad or coupon and one contrasting condition; map at least three complete melt pools and at least 500–1000 indexed grains. No additional powder. | Combine coarse whole-pool maps with 0.05–0.2 µm step-size maps at pool boundaries and centers. Report equiaxed fraction, grain size, aspect ratio, misorientation, and texture intensity. Sc/Zr systems also require nucleant-density considerations. (pqac-00000021, pqac-00000022, pqac-00000023, pqac-00000024, pqac-00000025) |
| 8 | XRD sin²ψ residual stress or released-cantilever deflection | Downstream thermo-mechanical stress and distortion validation; little direct leverage on melt-pool heat-source calibration | Three coupons or cantilevers at the selected condition. About 5–20 g fused; specimens can subsequently be reused for metallography. | Measure both in-plane directions at several positions and use appropriate X-ray elastic constants. For small Al coupons, release distortion may be more repeatable than absolute XRD because texture, weak diffraction, and uncertain stress-free spacing can dominate. (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036, pqac-00000041) |
| 9 | High-speed spatter and plume imaging, optionally with schlieren | Diagnosis of absorptivity transitions, vapor recoil, denudation, and unstable keyholing; optional for conduction-model calibration | Image at least three tracks in conduction, transition, and keyhole regimes while reusing the track matrix. Additional fused powder is negligible; about 2–5 g circulated. | Use at least 5–20 kfps for event counts and plume shape and preferably 50–100 kfps for droplet dynamics. Particularly useful for Mg- or Zn-bearing Al alloys, where evaporation may invalidate constant-absorptivity assumptions. (pqac-00000050, pqac-00000051, pqac-00000052, pqac-00000055) |
| — | Integrated minimum campaign | Sufficient independent data to calibrate a conduction heat source and validate multilayer printability without excessive fitting | About 25 track conditions, eight pads, and six to nine cubes or coupons. Target 40–80 g fused or consumed and 100–180 g maximum circulated, leaving reserve material from a 100–300 g lot. | Proceed sequentially: powder baseline, tracks, heat-source fit, pads, cubes, then microstructure and chemistry. Sieve reusable powder and retain virgin powder for comparisons. Defer EBSD, stress, and plume work until geometry and density meet predefined validation limits. |


*Table: Ranked measurements for calibrating and validating LPBF thermal and printability models for a new aluminium alloy while keeping total powder demand within a 100–300 g lot.*

{"answer": "## Experimental Measurement Methods for Calibrating and Validating LPBF Melt-Pool Models for New Aluminium and Copper Alloys

This review addresses nine categories of measurement needed to calibrate melt-pool and printability models—including the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing Module, Eagar–Tsai/Rosenthal analytical solutions, and CFD codes such as FLOW-3D—for new aluminium and copper alloys processed by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). The following summary table consolidates methods, equipment, standards, sampling, equations, uncertainties, and published references for each category.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

---

### 1. Melt-Pool Width, Depth and Length from Single-Track Cross-Sections

**Measurement method.** Single tracks are printed on a substrate (bare plate or with a nominal powder layer) across a matrix of laser power and scan speed. Each track is sectioned transversely (and at least one longitudinally), mounted, ground, polished (to 0.04 µm colloidal silica), and chemically etched. For Al–Si alloys (e.g., AlSi10Mg), Keller's reagent (2.5 mL HNO₃, 1.5 mL HCl, 1.0 mL HF, 95 mL H₂O) or Weck's reagent is standard; for Al–Cu and Al–Mg alloys, modified Keller's or Barker's electrolytic etch can be used. For Cu alloys, aqueous FeCl₃–HCl, ammonium persulfate, or Klemm-type colour etchants reveal the melt-pool boundary. At least 3–5 transverse sections per track are recommended because melt-pool depth varies substantially along a single track, especially near the keyhole threshold (pqac-00000001).

**Mode classification.** The depth-to-half-width criterion from King et al. classifies melt pools: keyholing occurs when d/(w/2) > 1, or equivalently d/w > 0.5 (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004). Conduction-mode pools are approximately semi-circular with d/w < 0.5. King et al. reported a normalized-enthalpy threshold for the conduction-to-keyhole transition of ΔH/h_s ≈ 30 ± 4 for 316L stainless steel, where ΔH/h_s = (AP)/(h_s √(πDvσ³)), with A the absorptivity, P laser power, h_s the enthalpy at melting, D thermal diffusivity, v scan speed, and σ beam radius (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002).

**Analytical model calibration.** The Eagar–Tsai model extends Rosenthal's moving point source to a Gaussian beam on a semi-infinite solid (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014). The quasi-steady temperature field is given by T(x,y,z) = T₀ + [AP/(ρcₚ(2π)^(3/2))] ∫₀^∞ g(τ′)dτ′, where g incorporates Gaussian spatial spreading. Melt-pool depth and half-width are obtained by finding the liquidus isotherm by root-finding. For calibration, absorptivity A is the primary fitting parameter; the beam radius σ should be measured independently (e.g., by beam profiler at D4σ) and fixed. Hong et al. demonstrated that fixing A independently (e.g., from Ye et al.'s closed-form correlation) converts the model from an object of calibration into one of validation; conduction-regime depths are reproduced to within a few percent, while keyhole tracks demand non-physical absorptivity values above unity (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014). For Goldak double-ellipsoid parameters used in FEM/CFD, the front and rear fractions (f_f + f_r = 2) and ellipsoid dimensions are typically optimized by BOBYQA or similar derivative-free methods against measured width, depth, and length (pqac-00000016).

**Thermo-Calc AM Module and open alternatives.** The Thermo-Calc AM Module uses CALPHAD-derived thermophysical properties (from its Property and Equilibrium modules) as inputs to a Scheil or equilibrium solidification path and an Eagar–Tsai-class thermal model. It predicts melt-pool geometry, solidification path, and susceptibility to cracking. The open-source printability framework of Sheikh et al. similarly uses CALPHAD data and calibrated Eagar–Tsai models, combining defect criteria with Bayesian model averaging to generate printability maps without proprietary code (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031).

**Open-source code.** 3DThesis (github.com/LLNL/ExaCA thermal kernel) provides open Eagar–Tsai melt-pool calculations. AdditiveFOAM is an open-source CFD solver for LPBF. The Honarmandi et al. Bayesian calibration framework for Eagar–Tsai has been described in detail (doi: 10.1016/j.addma.2021.102300).

---

### 2. Laser Absorptivity at ~1070 nm

**Calorimetric method (Trapp et al.).** Metal discs and ~100 µm powder layers are laser-irradiated while thermally isolated in a porous-alumina holder. The effective absorptivity is A_eff = E_abs/E_L, where E_abs = m∫C_p(T)dT is determined from the thermocouple-measured temperature rise and E_L = PL/v is the incident laser energy (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000015). At low power (conduction mode), powder absorptivity is approximately twice that of polished bare discs. After melting and track consolidation, absorptivity drops, then rises sharply at the keyhole transition due to multiple reflections within the vapor cavity (pqac-00000006).

**Integrating-sphere radiometry (Simonds et al., NIST).** A gold-coated integrating sphere with calibrated InGaAs photodiodes measures dynamic reflectance with sub-microsecond resolution. Absorbed power is P_abs(t) = P₀(t) − [P_head(t) + P_sphere(t)], and dynamic absorptance is A(t) = P_abs(t)/P₀(t) (pqac-00000007). This approach can resolve the precise moment of melt and keyhole formation.

**Typical values.** For pure Cu at 1070 nm: flat bulk A ≈ 0.03–0.05; Cu powder bed A ≈ 0.12–0.20 (4–5× bulk); at keyholing Cu powder absorptivity rises toward ~0.53 (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). For common structural alloys (which may include Al alloys), flat solid absorptivity is ~30% and powder ~60%; clean bulk aluminium at 1070 nm is ~5–9% (pqac-00000010). Uncertainty: calorimetry ±5–10% relative; integrating sphere a few percent after calibration (pqac-00000007).

---

### 3. Thermal History, G, R, and Cooling Rate

**Direct methods.** Thermocouples embedded in the substrate near tracks provide indirect cooling-rate data (bandwidth-limited, typically 10³–10⁴ K/s resolution). Two-colour pyrometry and calibrated IR thermography (MWIR/SWIR high-speed cameras) can measure melt-pool surface temperatures with ±2–5% accuracy under grey-body assumptions (pqac-00000018).

**Post-mortem proxies.** Cell or dendrite arm spacing λ relates to cooling rate Ṫ by a power law λ = A·Ṫ^(−n). The constants A and n must be determined for the specific alloy rather than imported from casting literature. For LPBF AlSi10Mg, cooling rates of 10⁵–10⁷ K/s are typical (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018). The local solidification rate at any point on the melt-pool boundary is R = v·cos β, where v is the scan speed and β is the angle between the scan direction and the local interface normal (pqac-00000019). The thermal gradient G is commonly estimated from Rosenthal or Eagar–Tsai solutions at the liquidus isotherm, yielding cooling rate Ṫ = G·R (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020).

**In-situ synchrotron X-ray imaging.** At facilities such as the APS 32-ID beamline, high-speed X-ray radiography (up to 1 MHz frame rate) directly images the melt pool, keyhole, solidification front, and pore dynamics during LPBF. This enables direct measurement of keyhole depth and fluctuation frequency (2.5–10 kHz), vapor-depression morphology, and solidification-front velocity (pqac-00000050).

---

### 4. Columnar-to-Equiaxed Transition, Grain Size and Texture

**EBSD methods.** Sections parallel to the build direction are prepared with final colloidal-silica or low-energy ion-beam polishing and mapped by field-emission SEM with EBSD. For Sc/Zr-modified Al alloys, the bimodal microstructure consists of fine equiaxed grains (FG) at melt-pool boundaries and coarser columnar grains (CG) in the pool centre. Lu et al. measured FG diameter of 0.45 ± 0.19 µm and CG width of 1.07 ± 0.49 µm, with equiaxed area fraction ~65% (pqac-00000021). Step sizes of 0.05–0.2 µm are needed for submicrometre Sc/Zr-refined grains.

**CET models and G–R maps.** The ratio G/R controls morphology: high G/R favours columnar growth, low G/R favours equiaxed. The critical G/R for CET depends on nucleant density and undercooling; in Sc/Zr systems, primary Al₃(Sc,Zr) particles provide heterogeneous nucleation sites with small lattice misfit to α-Al (pqac-00000022). Hunt's model defines a critical G below which the columnar front is blocked by equiaxed grains ahead of it, while the KGT (Kurz–Giovanola–Trivedi) model provides the dendrite-tip undercooling as a function of R. Plotted on G–R maps, CET boundaries delineate columnar, mixed, and equiaxed regions (pqac-00000023). Platform preheating (reducing G) and increased energy density have been shown to increase equiaxed fraction in Scalmalloy (pqac-00000025).

---

### 5. Composition Change by Selective Evaporation

**Measurement.** Virgin powder and printed coupons are dissolved and analyzed by ICP-OES (per ASTM E3061 for Al alloys). At least three independent digestions per condition are recommended (pqac-00000027). EPMA/WDS provides spatial composition maps; SEM-EDS is inadequate for detecting ~1% relative Mg loss.

**Evaporation modelling.** The Langmuir/Hertz–Knudsen equation gives the evaporative flux for each element: J_i = α_i · a_i · p_i^sat(T) · √[M_i/(2πRT)], integrated over the melt-pool surface area and lifetime, with corrections for inert-gas shielding (pqac-00000026). Bärtl et al. measured 7.9% total mass loss during electromagnetic levitation of Scalmalloy at ~540 K superheat, dominated by Mg evaporation (pqac-00000026). For Al–Zn alloys (e.g., 7xxx series), Zn and Mg loss has been documented with ICP-OES by Li et al. (pqac-00000027).

---

### 6. Printability Maps

**Construction workflow.** (i) Single-track experiments across 20–30 power–speed combinations identify conduction, transition, and keyhole regimes and balling. (ii) Single-layer pads at candidate hatch spacings test overlap and continuity. (iii) Multi-layer cubes (5–10 mm) validate density. Boundaries: lack of fusion occurs when melt-pool depth d < layer thickness t, or when the overlap criterion (h/W)² + (t/D)² > 1 is violated; keyhole porosity warning at d/w > 0.5; balling when the melt-pool length-to-width ratio L/W ≳ 2 and the track is discontinuous (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030).

**Density measurement.** Archimedes method (ASTM B962) provides bulk density but can exceed 100% due to wetting and uncertain theoretical density (pqac-00000034). Optical image analysis (ImageJ on ≥3 polished planes, per ASTM E1245) gives area-percent porosity; this method was preferred by Zhang et al. for its lower variability (pqac-00000034). Micro-CT distinguishes irregular LOF pores from rounded keyhole pores.

**Automated frameworks.** The Sheikh et al. framework uses CALPHAD-derived properties, Eagar–Tsai predictions, and Bayesian model averaging across 12 defect-criterion combinations to produce probabilistic printability maps for any alloy with CALPHAD data (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031).

---

### 7. Residual Stress in Small LPBF Coupons

**XRD sin²ψ.** A laboratory diffractometer (e.g., Stresstech G3) with appropriate radiation (Cr-Kα for Al (111)/(311), or Mn-Kα for Ni alloys) measures lattice spacing d at multiple ψ tilts (typically 11 angles spanning ±45°). Stress is calculated from the slope of d vs. sin²ψ using X-ray elastic constants (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036). Typical uncertainty for Al is ±20–50 MPa; texture, coarse grains, and uncertain stress-free d₀ can dominate.

**Bridge/cantilever deflection.** Alligator- or bridge-shaped cantilevers are printed, then partially released by wire EDM. The resulting deformation is measured by DIC or profilometry and compared with thermo-mechanical FE predictions (pqac-00000041). This approach is pragmatic for small desktop-scale coupons.

**Hole drilling.** Incremental drilling with strain gauges or ESPI (per ASTM E837) resolves depth-dependent stress to ~250 µm (pqac-00000035). The contour method (wire EDM cut, surface displacement by CMM or profilometry) provides a 2D stress map but requires larger specimens.

**Neutron diffraction.** Provides through-thickness lattice strain at millimetre spatial resolution (per ISO 21432) but requires beam time at a neutron facility (pqac-00000040).

---

### 8. Spatter and Vapour Plume

**High-speed imaging.** Side-view cameras at 5–60 kfps (e.g., Phantom V2512, Fastcam 1024 PCI at 6 kHz for AlSi10Mg) with narrow-band illumination (e.g., CAVILUX HF, Lumencor SOLA) capture spatter trajectories, velocities, and counts (pqac-00000051). Schlieren imaging uses a collimated source, knife edge, and high-speed camera to visualize vapour-plume density gradients and morphology (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000056).

**Relevance for Al.** In Mg-bearing Al alloys, vigorous Mg vaporization produces increased spatter, denudation, and oxide-rich fume (MgO) that can contaminate the powder bed and attenuate the laser (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000055). Guo et al. used synchrotron X-ray imaging at ESRF to correlate vapour-depression morphology with spatter dynamics in an Al–Fe–Zr alloy, showing that conduction-mode depressions produce backward spatter while keyhole rear walls redirect spatter vertically (pqac-00000050).

---

### 9. Powder Properties

**Particle size distribution.** Laser diffraction (ISO 13320) provides volume-weighted PSD; dynamic image analysis (ISO 13322) gives number-weighted PSD and shape parameters. Report D10, D50, D90, and span (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000045).

**Flowability.** Hall funnel (ASTM B213) and Carney funnel (ASTM B964) measure flow time; many fine Al powders show "no flow" through a Hall funnel. The FT4 powder rheometer provides dynamic flow energy, specific energy, and aeration response under conditions more representative of recoating (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000048). Rotating-drum analysers (GranuDrum, Revolution Analyzer) measure avalanche angle at recoater-relevant speeds (pqac-00000048). Combine multiple techniques (pqac-00000044).

**Density and chemistry.** Apparent density (ASTM B212), tap density (ASTM B527), and Hausner ratio HR = ρ_tap/ρ_bulk characterize packing (pqac-00000044). Oxygen and hydrogen content are measured by inert-gas fusion (ASTM E1019 for O/N, ASTM E1447 for H in applicable materials) using a LECO-type analyzer (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046). Moisture is assessed by Karl Fischer titration or TGA.

---

### 10. Ranked Minimum Measurement Set for AM Module Calibration with ~100–300 g of Powder

The following table provides a prioritized campaign for calibrating and validating an Eagar–Tsai-class or Thermo-Calc AM Module model for a new Al alloy, designed to consume no more than 40–80 g of powder while circulating up to 100–180 g.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

**Recommended workflow.** Proceed sequentially: (1) baseline powder characterization; (2) single-track matrix on bare plates and powder layers; (3) absorptivity fitting and Eagar–Tsai calibration against measured width and depth; (4) single-layer pads to validate overlap; (5) small cubes for multilayer density; (6) reuse sections for cell-spacing cooling-rate estimation and ICP-OES composition check; (7) EBSD for CET on nominal and contrasting conditions; (8) XRD or cantilever for stress if needed; (9) optional high-speed imaging for diagnostic purposes. Sieve and retain reusable powder at each stage, and preserve an unopened baseline aliquot for comparison.

---

### Key References with DOIs

{"answer": "## Experimental Measurement Methods for Calibrating and Validating LPBF Melt-Pool Models for New Aluminium and Copper Alloys

This review addresses nine categories of measurement needed to calibrate melt-pool and printability models—including the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing Module, Eagar–Tsai/Rosenthal analytical solutions, and CFD codes such as FLOW-3D—for new aluminium and copper alloys processed by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF). The following summary table consolidates methods, equipment, standards, sampling, equations, uncertainties, and published references for each category.

<artifact id="artifact-00"/>

---

### 1. Melt-Pool Width, Depth and Length from Single-Track Cross-Sections

**Measurement method.** Single tracks are printed on a substrate (bare plate or with a nominal powder layer) across a matrix of laser power and scan speed. Each track is sectioned transversely (and at least one longitudinally), mounted, ground, polished (to 0.04 µm colloidal silica), and chemically etched. For Al–Si alloys (e.g., AlSi10Mg), Keller's reagent (2.5 mL HNO₃, 1.5 mL HCl, 1.0 mL HF, 95 mL H₂O) or Weck's reagent is standard; for Al–Cu and Al–Mg alloys, modified Keller's or Barker's electrolytic etch can be used. For Cu alloys, aqueous FeCl₃–HCl, ammonium persulfate, or Klemm-type colour etchants reveal the melt-pool boundary. At least 3–5 transverse sections per track are recommended because melt-pool depth varies substantially along a single track, especially near the keyhole threshold (pqac-00000001).

**Mode classification.** The depth-to-half-width criterion from King et al. classifies melt pools: keyholing occurs when d/(w/2) > 1, or equivalently d/w > 0.5 (pqac-00000000, pqac-00000003, pqac-00000004). Conduction-mode pools are approximately semi-circular with d/w < 0.5. King et al. reported a normalized-enthalpy threshold for the conduction-to-keyhole transition of ΔH/h_s ≈ 30 ± 4 for 316L stainless steel, where ΔH/h_s = (AP)/(h_s √(πDvσ³)), with A the absorptivity, P laser power, h_s the enthalpy at melting, D thermal diffusivity, v scan speed, and σ beam radius (pqac-00000001, pqac-00000002).

**Analytical model calibration.** The Eagar–Tsai model extends Rosenthal's moving point source to a Gaussian beam on a semi-infinite solid (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014). The quasi-steady temperature field is given by T(x,y,z) = T₀ + [AP/(ρcₚ(2π)^(3/2))] ∫₀^∞ g(τ′)dτ′, where g incorporates Gaussian spatial spreading. Melt-pool depth and half-width are obtained by finding the liquidus isotherm by root-finding. For calibration, absorptivity A is the primary fitting parameter; the beam radius σ should be measured independently (e.g., by beam profiler at D4σ) and fixed. Hong et al. demonstrated that fixing A independently (e.g., from Ye et al.'s closed-form correlation) converts the model from an object of calibration into one of validation; conduction-regime depths are reproduced to within a few percent, while keyhole tracks demand non-physical absorptivity values above unity (pqac-00000012, pqac-00000014). For Goldak double-ellipsoid parameters used in FEM/CFD, the front and rear fractions (f_f + f_r = 2) and ellipsoid dimensions are typically optimized by BOBYQA or similar derivative-free methods against measured width, depth, and length (pqac-00000016).

**Thermo-Calc AM Module and open alternatives.** The Thermo-Calc AM Module uses CALPHAD-derived thermophysical properties (from its Property and Equilibrium modules) as inputs to a Scheil or equilibrium solidification path and an Eagar–Tsai-class thermal model. It predicts melt-pool geometry, solidification path, and susceptibility to cracking. The open-source printability framework of Sheikh et al. similarly uses CALPHAD data and calibrated Eagar–Tsai models, combining defect criteria with Bayesian model averaging to generate printability maps without proprietary code (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031).

**Open-source code.** 3DThesis (github.com/LLNL/ExaCA thermal kernel) provides open Eagar–Tsai melt-pool calculations. AdditiveFOAM is an open-source CFD solver for LPBF. The Honarmandi et al. Bayesian calibration framework for Eagar–Tsai has been described in detail (doi: 10.1016/j.addma.2021.102300).

---

### 2. Laser Absorptivity at ~1070 nm

**Calorimetric method (Trapp et al.).** Metal discs and ~100 µm powder layers are laser-irradiated while thermally isolated in a porous-alumina holder. The effective absorptivity is A_eff = E_abs/E_L, where E_abs = m∫C_p(T)dT is determined from the thermocouple-measured temperature rise and E_L = PL/v is the incident laser energy (pqac-00000006, pqac-00000015). At low power (conduction mode), powder absorptivity is approximately twice that of polished bare discs. After melting and track consolidation, absorptivity drops, then rises sharply at the keyhole transition due to multiple reflections within the vapor cavity (pqac-00000006).

**Integrating-sphere radiometry (Simonds et al., NIST).** A gold-coated integrating sphere with calibrated InGaAs photodiodes measures dynamic reflectance with sub-microsecond resolution. Absorbed power is P_abs(t) = P₀(t) − [P_head(t) + P_sphere(t)], and dynamic absorptance is A(t) = P_abs(t)/P₀(t) (pqac-00000007). This approach can resolve the precise moment of melt and keyhole formation.

**Typical values.** For pure Cu at 1070 nm: flat bulk A ≈ 0.03–0.05; Cu powder bed A ≈ 0.12–0.20 (4–5× bulk); at keyholing Cu powder absorptivity rises toward ~0.53 (pqac-00000005, pqac-00000009, pqac-00000010). For common structural alloys (which may include Al alloys), flat solid absorptivity is ~30% and powder ~60%; clean bulk aluminium at 1070 nm is ~5–9% (pqac-00000010). Uncertainty: calorimetry ±5–10% relative; integrating sphere a few percent after calibration (pqac-00000007).

---

### 3. Thermal History, G, R, and Cooling Rate

**Direct methods.** Thermocouples embedded in the substrate near tracks provide indirect cooling-rate data (bandwidth-limited, typically 10³–10⁴ K/s resolution). Two-colour pyrometry and calibrated IR thermography (MWIR/SWIR high-speed cameras) can measure melt-pool surface temperatures with ±2–5% accuracy under grey-body assumptions (pqac-00000018).

**Post-mortem proxies.** Cell or dendrite arm spacing λ relates to cooling rate Ṫ by a power law λ = A·Ṫ^(−n). The constants A and n must be determined for the specific alloy rather than imported from casting literature. For LPBF AlSi10Mg, cooling rates of 10⁵–10⁷ K/s are typical (pqac-00000017, pqac-00000018). The local solidification rate at any point on the melt-pool boundary is R = v·cos β, where v is the scan speed and β is the angle between the scan direction and the local interface normal (pqac-00000019). The thermal gradient G is commonly estimated from Rosenthal or Eagar–Tsai solutions at the liquidus isotherm, yielding cooling rate Ṫ = G·R (pqac-00000019, pqac-00000020).

**In-situ synchrotron X-ray imaging.** At facilities such as the APS 32-ID beamline, high-speed X-ray radiography (up to 1 MHz frame rate) directly images the melt pool, keyhole, solidification front, and pore dynamics during LPBF. This enables direct measurement of keyhole depth and fluctuation frequency (2.5–10 kHz), vapor-depression morphology, and solidification-front velocity (pqac-00000050).

---

### 4. Columnar-to-Equiaxed Transition, Grain Size and Texture

**EBSD methods.** Sections parallel to the build direction are prepared with final colloidal-silica or low-energy ion-beam polishing and mapped by field-emission SEM with EBSD. For Sc/Zr-modified Al alloys, the bimodal microstructure consists of fine equiaxed grains (FG) at melt-pool boundaries and coarser columnar grains (CG) in the pool centre. Lu et al. measured FG diameter of 0.45 ± 0.19 µm and CG width of 1.07 ± 0.49 µm, with equiaxed area fraction ~65% (pqac-00000021). Step sizes of 0.05–0.2 µm are needed for submicrometre Sc/Zr-refined grains.

**CET models and G–R maps.** The ratio G/R controls morphology: high G/R favours columnar growth, low G/R favours equiaxed. The critical G/R for CET depends on nucleant density and undercooling; in Sc/Zr systems, primary Al₃(Sc,Zr) particles provide heterogeneous nucleation sites with small lattice misfit to α-Al (pqac-00000022). Hunt's model defines a critical G below which the columnar front is blocked by equiaxed grains ahead of it, while the KGT (Kurz–Giovanola–Trivedi) model provides the dendrite-tip undercooling as a function of R. Plotted on G–R maps, CET boundaries delineate columnar, mixed, and equiaxed regions (pqac-00000023). Platform preheating (reducing G) and increased energy density have been shown to increase equiaxed fraction in Scalmalloy (pqac-00000025).

---

### 5. Composition Change by Selective Evaporation

**Measurement.** Virgin powder and printed coupons are dissolved and analyzed by ICP-OES (per ASTM E3061 for Al alloys). At least three independent digestions per condition are recommended (pqac-00000027). EPMA/WDS provides spatial composition maps; SEM-EDS is inadequate for detecting ~1% relative Mg loss.

**Evaporation modelling.** The Langmuir/Hertz–Knudsen equation gives the evaporative flux for each element: J_i = α_i · a_i · p_i^sat(T) · √[M_i/(2πRT)], integrated over the melt-pool surface area and lifetime, with corrections for inert-gas shielding (pqac-00000026). Bärtl et al. measured 7.9% total mass loss during electromagnetic levitation of Scalmalloy at ~540 K superheat, dominated by Mg evaporation (pqac-00000026). For Al–Zn alloys (e.g., 7xxx series), Zn and Mg loss has been documented with ICP-OES by Li et al. (pqac-00000027).

---

### 6. Printability Maps

**Construction workflow.** (i) Single-track experiments across 20–30 power–speed combinations identify conduction, transition, and keyhole regimes and balling. (ii) Single-layer pads at candidate hatch spacings test overlap and continuity. (iii) Multi-layer cubes (5–10 mm) validate density. Boundaries: lack of fusion occurs when melt-pool depth d < layer thickness t, or when the overlap criterion (h/W)² + (t/D)² > 1 is violated; keyhole porosity warning at d/w > 0.5; balling when the melt-pool length-to-width ratio L/W ≳ 2 and the track is discontinuous (pqac-00000028, pqac-00000029, pqac-00000030).

**Density measurement.** Archimedes method (ASTM B962) provides bulk density but can exceed 100% due to wetting and uncertain theoretical density (pqac-00000034). Optical image analysis (ImageJ on ≥3 polished planes, per ASTM E1245) gives area-percent porosity; this method was preferred by Zhang et al. for its lower variability (pqac-00000034). Micro-CT distinguishes irregular LOF pores from rounded keyhole pores.

**Automated frameworks.** The Sheikh et al. framework uses CALPHAD-derived properties, Eagar–Tsai predictions, and Bayesian model averaging across 12 defect-criterion combinations to produce probabilistic printability maps for any alloy with CALPHAD data (pqac-00000029, pqac-00000031).

---

### 7. Residual Stress in Small LPBF Coupons

**XRD sin²ψ.** A laboratory diffractometer (e.g., Stresstech G3) with appropriate radiation (Cr-Kα for Al (111)/(311), or Mn-Kα for Ni alloys) measures lattice spacing d at multiple ψ tilts (typically 11 angles spanning ±45°). Stress is calculated from the slope of d vs. sin²ψ using X-ray elastic constants (pqac-00000035, pqac-00000036). Typical uncertainty for Al is ±20–50 MPa; texture, coarse grains, and uncertain stress-free d₀ can dominate.

**Bridge/cantilever deflection.** Alligator- or bridge-shaped cantilevers are printed, then partially released by wire EDM. The resulting deformation is measured by DIC or profilometry and compared with thermo-mechanical FE predictions (pqac-00000041). This approach is pragmatic for small desktop-scale coupons.

**Hole drilling.** Incremental drilling with strain gauges or ESPI (per ASTM E837) resolves depth-dependent stress to ~250 µm (pqac-00000035). The contour method (wire EDM cut, surface displacement by CMM or profilometry) provides a 2D stress map but requires larger specimens.

**Neutron diffraction.** Provides through-thickness lattice strain at millimetre spatial resolution (per ISO 21432) but requires beam time at a neutron facility (pqac-00000040).

---

### 8. Spatter and Vapour Plume

**High-speed imaging.** Side-view cameras at 5–60 kfps (e.g., Phantom V2512, Fastcam 1024 PCI at 6 kHz for AlSi10Mg) with narrow-band illumination (e.g., CAVILUX HF, Lumencor SOLA) capture spatter trajectories, velocities, and counts (pqac-00000051). Schlieren imaging uses a collimated source, knife edge, and high-speed camera to visualize vapour-plume density gradients and morphology (pqac-00000054, pqac-00000056).

**Relevance for Al.** In Mg-bearing Al alloys, vigorous Mg vaporization produces increased spatter, denudation, and oxide-rich fume (MgO) that can contaminate the powder bed and attenuate the laser (pqac-00000053, pqac-00000055). Guo et al. used synchrotron X-ray imaging at ESRF to correlate vapour-depression morphology with spatter dynamics in an Al–Fe–Zr alloy, showing that conduction-mode depressions produce backward spatter while keyhole rear walls redirect spatter vertically (pqac-00000050).

---

### 9. Powder Properties

**Particle size distribution.** Laser diffraction (ISO 13320) provides volume-weighted PSD; dynamic image analysis (ISO 13322) gives number-weighted PSD and shape parameters. Report D10, D50, D90, and span (pqac-00000043, pqac-00000045).

**Flowability.** Hall funnel (ASTM B213) and Carney funnel (ASTM B964) measure flow time; many fine Al powders show "no flow" through a Hall funnel. The FT4 powder rheometer provides dynamic flow energy, specific energy, and aeration response under conditions more representative of recoating (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000048). Rotating-drum analysers (GranuDrum, Revolution Analyzer) measure avalanche angle at recoater-relevant speeds (pqac-00000048). Combine multiple techniques (pqac-00000044).

**Density and chemistry.** Apparent density (ASTM B212), tap density (ASTM B527), and Hausner ratio HR = ρ_tap/ρ_bulk characterize packing (pqac-00000044). Oxygen and hydrogen content are measured by inert-gas fusion (ASTM E1019 for O/N, ASTM E1447 for H in applicable materials) using a LECO-type analyzer (pqac-00000045, pqac-00000046). Moisture is assessed by Karl Fischer titration or TGA.

---

### 10. Ranked Minimum Measurement Set for AM Module Calibration with ~100–300 g of Powder

The following table provides a prioritized campaign for calibrating and validating an Eagar–Tsai-class or Thermo-Calc AM Module model for a new Al alloy, designed to consume no more than 40–80 g of powder while circulating up to 100–180 g.

<artifact id="artifact-01"/>

**Recommended workflow.** Proceed sequentially: (1) baseline powder characterization; (2) single-track matrix on bare plates and powder layers; (3) absorptivity fitting and Eagar–Tsai calibration against measured width and depth; (4) single-layer pads to validate overlap; (5) small cubes for multilayer density; (6) reuse sections for cell-spacing cooling-rate estimation and ICP-OES composition check; (7) EBSD for CET on nominal and contrasting conditions; (8) XRD or cantilever for stress if needed; (9) optional high-speed imaging for diagnostic purposes. Sieve and retain reusable powder at each stage, and preserve an unopened baseline aliquot for comparison.

---

### Key References with DOIs

state.question:
We want to measure, for new aluminium alloys (and some copper alloys) printed by laser powder bed fusion (LPBF), the quantities that the Thermo-Calc Additive Manufacturing Module and similar melt-pool models predict, so we can calibrate and validate them. Our printing is small-scale: single tracks, single-layer pads, and small cubes/coupons (desktop LPBF with a 200-500 W, 1070 nm fiber laser, ~50-100 um spot; plus an Aconity MIDI and a Concept Laser M2 elsewhere). Alloys: AlSi10Mg, Al-Mg-Sc-Zr (Scalmalloy-type), lean Al-Mg-Zr, Al-Mn, Al-Ce and Al-Cu alloys, and Cu alloys (Ni-Al bronze, Cu-Ni). Please review the peer-reviewed literature and, for each item below, give the measurement method(s), typical equipment, sample preparation, how many tracks/samples are needed, the analysis (with equations), the open-source code available, typical uncertainties, and published examples with DOIs (prefer Al and Cu alloys):

1. Melt pool width, depth and length from single-track cross-sections and top-view imaging: etchants for Al and Cu alloys, number of sections per track, conduction vs transition vs keyhole mode classification (depth/width ratio, normalized enthalpy deltaH/h_s from King et al., keyhole number / Ke from Gan et al.), and heat-source calibration (absorptivity, beam radius, Goldak/Gaussian parameters) against measured melt pools, including how the Thermo-Calc AM Module, Eagar-Tsai / Rosenthal models and FLOW-3D type CFD have been calibrated.
2. Laser absorptivity of Al and Cu powder beds and bulk at ~1070 nm: integrating-sphere and calorimetric methods (e.g., Trapp et al. LLNL, NIST integrating-sphere work), values vs power/speed/mode.
3. Thermal history, peak temperature, thermal gradient G and solidification rate R: thermocouples, two-colour pyrometry, IR thermography, and post-mortem proxies (cell/dendrite arm spacing vs cooling rate relations for Al-Si and Al-Mg alloys, R = v cos(theta) from melt-pool shape), and in-situ synchrotron X-ray imaging/diffraction (e.g., Advanced Photon Source 32-ID) measurements of melt pool, keyhole and solidification.
4. Columnar-to-equiaxed transition, grain size and texture in LPBF Al alloys (Sc/Zr inoculation): EBSD on tracks and pads, comparison with G-R maps and Hunt/KGT-type CET models.
5. Composition change by selective evaporation (Mg, Zn, Li loss in Al alloys; Zn in brasses): ICP-OES/EDS/EPMA of powder vs printed material, measured Mg loss vs energy density, comparison with evaporation models.
6. Printability maps: lack of fusion, keyholing, balling and hot cracking criteria; density (Archimedes, CT, optical image analysis) vs process parameters; keyhole porosity thresholds; crack density measurement; how to build printability maps from single tracks and pads with minimal powder.
7. Residual stress in small LPBF coupons: XRD sin^2(psi), bridge-curvature / cantilever deflection, contour method, hole drilling, neutron diffraction.
8. Spatter and vapour plume: high-speed imaging and schlieren, and their relevance for Al.
9. Powder properties that control LPBF of these alloys: particle size distribution (laser diffraction vs image analysis, ISO 13322 / ISO 13320), flowability (Hall/Carney, revolution powder analysis, FT4, avalanche/GranuDrum), apparent/tap density, oxygen and hydrogen content (inert gas fusion, ASTM E1019 / E1447), moisture.

End with a ranked list of the minimum set of single-track, pad and coupon measurements that best calibrates the AM module (or open alternatives) for a new Al alloy with only ~100-300 g of powder, and give a full reference list with DOIs.

6. Printability maps: lack of fusion, keyholing, balling and hot cracking criteria; density (Archimedes, CT, optical image analysis) vs process parameters; keyhole porosity thresholds; crack density measurement; how to build printability maps from single tracks and pads with minimal powder.
7. Residual stress in small LPBF coupons: XRD sin^2(psi), bridge-curvature / cantilever deflection, contour method, hole drilling, neutron diffraction.
8. Spatter and vapour plume: high-speed imaging and schlieren, and their relevance for Al.
9. Powder properties that control LPBF of these alloys: particle size distribution (laser diffraction vs image analysis, ISO 13322 / ISO 13320), flowability (Hall/Carney, revolution powder analysis, FT4, avalanche/GranuDrum), apparent/tap density, oxygen and hydrogen content (inert gas fusion, ASTM E1019 / E1447), moisture.

End with a ranked list of the minimum set of single-track, pad and coupon measurements that best calibrates the AM module (or open alternatives) for a new Al alloy with only ~100-300 g of powder, and give a full reference list with DOIs.
